🚨 CFR | CHICAGO 2027 MAYORAL RACE — PETITION CHALLENGE

Danielle Carter-Walters’ mayoral nominating petitions have been challenged by:

* Patricia Rae Easley
* Rickey Hendon
* Earl C. Williams Jr.

Chicago Flips Red (CFR) was physically present at the Chicago Board of Elections on November 2, 2026, and personally observed these three names listed on the objection paperwork.

The individuals named are reportedly associated with Willie Wilson’s mayoral campaign.

WHO IS RICKEY HENDON?

Rickey Hendon is a former Chicago 27th Ward alderman (1991–1993) and former Illinois state senator (1993–2011). He has a documented history of working with Willie Wilson’s political campaigns.

The Chicago Sun-Times reported on October 26, 2026, that Hendon was handling petition challenges for Wilson’s 2027 mayoral campaign.

In December 2022, The TRiiBE reported allegations involving a recorded conversation in which Hendon allegedly offered financial compensation to have a petition challenge against Willie Wilson withdrawn. Wilson’s campaign acknowledged Hendon’s voice on the recording but stated that his comments were unauthorized.

WHAT HAPPENED TODAY?

November 2, 2026, was the deadline for filing objections to Chicago’s 2027 municipal candidates.

CFR witnessed the objection paperwork naming Patricia Rae Easley, Rickey Hendon, and Earl C. Williams Jr. against Danielle Carter-Walters.

The objectors allege that Carter-Walters does not have enough valid petition signatures to qualify for Chicago’s 2027 mayoral ballot.

This is an allegation made by the objectors, not a determination that Carter-Walters failed to qualify.

An objection does not automatically disqualify a candidate. The Chicago Electoral Board must review the challenged signatures and determine whether her nominating petitions satisfy the legal requirements.

PRESIDENT TRUMP ANNOUNCES $1 MILLION VOTER FRAUD REWARD

On October 26, 2026, President Donald Trump announced that individuals reporting voter fraud in past elections or the upcoming 2026 midterm elections would receive $1,000,000 if their reports lead to the arrest and conviction of those responsible.

CFR will continue monitoring the objection proceedings, the individuals involved, their connections to Willie Wilson’s mayoral campaign, and election accountability in Chicago.

text:
8 PM Top-of-the-Hour News

It's Election Day eve - and the candidates are making their closing arguments
In South Carolina - Democrat Annie Andrews told supporters South Carolina has a chance to lead by example: “In that moment, South Carolina will show the entire country that we here proudly in South Carolina finally figured out how to work together and move forward together past this hyper divisive, hyper partisan era of politics. ”
Andrews is battling Republican Darline Graham - the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed says the election is the moment to start making the country stronger: “If we're willing to reach across the divides they tell us we can't breach, divides of race, of faith, of geography, sexual orientation, gender identity. We can build together what we can't have alone. The lesson of solidarity is the idea. That alone we might be weak, but collectively we are strong. ”
El-Sayed is up against Former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers.

The Supreme Court is denying the Trump Administration's appeal in California's mail-in ballot case.   At issue were 20-thousand ballots the feds say may have been cast by non-US citizens. The Supreme Court did not explain its decision tonight.

President Trump highlighted a sharp drop in energy costs during his final election eve pitch today, directly linking the market shift to his administration's foreign policy actions.: “Oil prices are plunging now. They're plunging, a record. Nobody's ever seen a plunge like this, and they'll be down. I hope people realize that when they go into the voting booth, because we had to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon. If we allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, this country could never function the same way. ”
Global oil prices tumbled over seven percent today.

The Kennedy Center has announced this year's class of Lifetime Achievement honorees.: “5 artists will receive the 49th Kennedy Center Honors this year, including singer Paul Anka. Music producer David Foster, playwright David Memet, actor Andy Garcia, my advice to you again is this run and hide and country star Barbara Mandrell. They'll be celebrated December 7th, but for the first time, the ceremony won't be held at the Kennedy Center. Instead, the gala is moving to nearby Capital One Arena, Stacy Lynn Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

We're learning more about the final moments before a private LearJet crashed in Florida yesterday, killing all 9 people on board.   NewsNation's Connell McShane with the latest: “Radar data showing that the plane dropped over 30,000 ft at the time of the crash, left a massive crater near a mobile home park in Palm Beach County, and there was a short time ago where NTSB officials came out and said they're looking at weather conditions at the time the crash happened, and forecasters say there's heavy rain and thunderstorms occurring in the area at the time. We're learning more as well about the identity of the co-pilot, 20 years old, a 20-year-old named Natalia Alfiguera. Her mother says she got her pilot's license when she was only 17 years old. ”
The NTSB says evidence shows the plane began breaking up in midair before crashing.

The trial started today for 2 baseball pitchers accused of a gambling conspiracy.: “Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Classe and Luis Ortiz face charges they colluded with gamblers who made hundreds of thousands of dollars betting on individual pitches. Their careers and possibly their freedom are at stake in the jury trial in Brooklyn federal court. Both have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges. Class A is the Guardian's former closer. Ortiz was a starter when they were charged in November of last year, Bill Rakoff, Worldwide News Network. ”

Weeks after her murder trial for killing her three children ended in a mistrial, Lindsay Clancy was back in a Massachusetts courtroom today.
Her lawyers are arguing the charges should be dismissed, because her postpartum psychosis made her strangle her kids. Prosecutors could seek to retry her or offer a plea deal.

text:
Porn star CJ Miles came to America with a one way ticket and $100 from her dad. The man waiting for her in Texas was 27, lived in his mom's basement and was secretly still married. He choked her every day, and the only people who tried to save her were his own mother and sister.

She grew up in the Philippines, and that is where he started dating her, while he still had a wife back home. He brought her over on a fiance visa. She had 90 days to marry him, no social security number, no job, and no one in the country but him.

Once she was in his house, he cut her off from everything. Every day he unplugged the computer so she couldn't talk to anyone back home. He told her straight to her face that she had nowhere to go because she didn't know anybody but him. Then the beatings started. She says he choked her left and right.

It got so bad that his own mother and sister wrote to immigration behind his back and told them their son was beating her. She still couldn't leave. Her $100 was long gone, and without papers she couldn't get a job.

Then a friend in Las Vegas told her to come out and offered her work. She told him she had a modeling gig, packed her bag and walked out. He never even came looking for her. Her friend picked her up at the airport and drove her straight to the Rhino strip club, where she ended up working for 12 years before she got into porn.

Today she tells the whole story herself on Holly Randall's podcast.

He told her she had nowhere to go, and she proved him wrong with one plane ticket.

Was she brave for walking out with nothing, or should her family never have put her on that plane alone?

text:
THE LAST FLIGHT OUT OF AUSTIN

A private aviation mystery. Two crashes. Two investigations. And questions that deserve answers.

June 16, 2026.

A Cessna Citation Latitude was flying over Texas with Joshua Baer, founder of Capital Factory, aboard.

The crew noticed an unusual vibration and humming noise. Then came fuel-system warnings and electrical problems.

They contacted maintenance. The vibration appeared to subside. The flight continued.

Then the situation deteriorated.

The aircraft diverted toward Laredo. One engine lost power during the approach. The other followed. The pilots attempted an emergency landing on a highway.

Baer died. Five other people aboard survived.

Investigators later identified a fractured fuel-tube assembly and damage to the starter-generator. Why the second engine also lost power remains unanswered.

November 1, 2026.

A Learjet 60 departed Austin for the Bahamas.

On board were Adam Robinson, founder of https://t.co/u4Vg9Qk66h and RB2B, his wife Helen, their two young children, a nanny, two family friends and two pilots.

Nine people.

The crew reported icing and moderate turbulence and requested an altitude change.

Then the aircraft began a catastrophic descent from approximately 35,000 feet. Within roughly a minute, it had lost more than 26,000 feet.

Investigators are examining evidence that the aircraft may have broken apart before impact.

All nine people aboard died.

TWO CRASHES. TWO AIRCRAFT. TWO OPERATORS. DIFFERENT INVESTIGATIONS.

The first centers on mechanical failures, maintenance and the loss of both engines.

The second centers on weather, icing, aircraft control and possible structural breakup.

There is no established connection between the accidents and no evidence of a common cause.

But the questions are unavoidable.

How are private aircraft maintained? How are mechanical warnings handled? Who decides when weather is too dangerous? What oversight applies to fractional ownership and charter operators?

Private aviation offers convenience, privacy and speed. It does not offer immunity from mechanical failure, weather or human error.

Investigators now face the difficult task of reconstructing two final flights, component by component and decision by decision.

There are no neat endings. Only families grieving and questions that deserve answers.

The most important part of any flight is what happens when something goes wrong.

Based on preliminary reporting and investigation information available November 2, 2026. Neither accident has an established final probable cause.

text:
Washington made it illegal to fake someone's voice or face with AI. Here's what that means for you.

If you live in Washington, or you're a creator worried about AI cloning your voice, read this.

On June 11, 2026, Washington's personality rights law picked up something new. It's called a "forged digital likeness."

That's a fake video, photo, or audio recording of a real person. It was made or changed with digital tools like AI. To count, it has to pass three tests:

• It looks or sounds real enough that you can't tell the difference.
• It puts words in your mouth or shows you doing something you didn't do.
• It's convincing enough to fool a regular person.

Here's what makes this law different.

It covers everyone. You don't have to be famous. Your voice doesn't have to be worth money. Living or dead, you're covered.

It's not just about ads. Most states only step in when someone uses you to sell something. Washington goes further. It covers merch, fundraising, and donation asks. It covers nonprofit and noncommercial uses too.

It has teeth. A court can order the fake taken down. You can go after your actual losses, any money they made off you, and your lawyer fees. The civil penalty doubled to $3,000. And you can get damages for emotional harm, humiliation, and damage to your reputation. Most states don't offer that.

There's a criminal side too. In Washington, it's already a crime to share a fake of someone to defraud, harass, or threaten them.

Why this matters to me. My voice is my work. I've spent over 20 years speaking out about cults and abuse. Survivors already get doubted. A fake clip of a survivor "saying" something they never said can do real damage. Now there's a law that says no.

If someone clones you:

1. Save everything. Screenshots, links, dates.
2. Report it to the platform.
3. Talk to an attorney who handles personality rights.
4. If it's harassing or threatening, report it to police.

What's still unsettled: Courts haven't tested how this law fits with free speech, parody, and satire yet. Expect it to be challenged.

And there's still no federal law. The NO FAKES Act is waiting on a full Senate vote. Until then, protection depends on what state you're in.

I'm not a lawyer, and this isn't legal advice. But you deserve to know your rights

Share this with a creator who needs it. 

#AIDeepfakes #VoiceCloning #CreatorRights #WashingtonState #SurvivorAdvocacy

text:
Donald Trump belongs to a long tradition of American politicians convinced that taxing imports is a recipe for national prosperity.

Alexander Hamilton, Henry Clay, John Quincy Adams, Abraham Lincoln, William McKinley, Benjamin Harrison, Theodore Roosevelt, William Howard Taft, Warren Harding, Calvin Coolidge and Herbert Hoover all supported protective tariffs to varying degrees. More recently, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden adopted selective protectionist measures.

Different centuries, different parties, different excuses. The same seductive economic fallacy: make foreign goods more expensive and Americans will somehow become richer.

Hamilton gave protectionism intellectual respectability in 1791. Clay built his American System around it. Lincoln defended protective tariffs. McKinley made them a political trademark. Hoover signed Smoot-Hawley in 1930, despite more than a thousand economists warning him against it.

Smoot-Hawley provoked retaliation and contributed to the collapse of international trade during the Great Depression. It did not cause the Depression, but it certainly offered no cure.

The fundamental economic mistake is horribly persistent.

A tariff does not create wealth. It changes prices, redistributes income and interferes with the international division of labour.

When Washington taxes imported steel, American steelmakers may benefit. American car manufacturers, machinery producers and construction companies face higher costs. Consumers pay more. Exporters risk retaliation. Politically connected industries receive protection while everyone else finances the privilege.

And politicians announce that they have saved American jobs.

What they rarely calculate are the jobs lost elsewhere, the investments never made, the businesses rendered uncompetitive and the purchasing power destroyed.

The evidence is hardly reassuring. Research published in the Journal of Economic Perspectives found that Trump’s 2018 tariffs were passed through into American import prices, reducing aggregate US real income by approximately $1.4 billion per month by the end of that year.

Protectionists invariably invoke America’s nineteenth-century industrialisation. But America also possessed abundant resources, extraordinary entrepreneurial energy, massive immigration, technological innovation and expanding domestic markets. Industrialisation happened under tariffs. That does not demonstrate that tariffs produced it.

Strategic industries and national security present more serious arguments for selective intervention. But even there, protection has costs, and politicians have powerful incentives to redefine every politically influential industry as strategically indispensable.

The deeper problem is political arrogance: the conviction that politicians know better than millions of consumers and entrepreneurs where capital, labour and resources should go.

Two centuries of protectionism have repeatedly demonstrated how easily economic policy becomes an auction of privileges.

Trump did not invent this doctrine. He inherited one of America’s oldest political temptations: confusing the prosperity of protected producers with the prosperity of an entire nation.

text:
The Trump administration on Monday signaled a negotiated deal with Iran was possible after Tehran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, albeit under strict conditions, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was said to still be lobbying for a resumption of attacks.

“Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK, down almost $10 a Barrel, A RECORD, because people feel that there will not be a War with Iran. Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!” US President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social a day before the midterm elections, in which a top issue has been the rise in energy prices since fighting began earlier this year with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

Trump in recent weeks had hinted about renewing attacks on Iran when voting ends Tuesday in the United States. But while speaking at the Washington Reflecting Pool on Monday, he indicated he might be thinking otherwise, resuming a pattern of alternating between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal.

Asked by reporters if he was considering striking Iran after the midterms, Trump replied “no,” though he has also previously played down the prospect of attacks before ordering them.

Vice President JD Vance meanwhile reported that there had been “a number of good conversations with the Iranians.”

“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance told reporters, adding that he discussed the issue with Trump an hour earlier. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”

“We’re going to keep on working at it… The Iranians are always a little unpredictable,” he said.

Trump “retains kinetic options, he retains non-kinetic options, but we certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more,” Vance continued.

Asked whether the US has given Iran a deadline before Trump makes due on threats to resume strikes, Vance said that the US has not given such constraints.

The vice president went on to claim that the US has already destroyed Iran’s nuclear program — even though Trump still talks about the possible need to bomb a number of other nuclear enrichment sites and even though Iran still maintains a stockpile of highly-enriched uranium.

“Having destroyed their nuclear program, we want to make sure they don’t rebuild it or try to rebuild it. That’s what matters most to the United States,” Vance said. In the past, he has said Washington’s main priority is restoring the flow of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, whose effective closure by Iran has led global gas prices to spike.

“They care a lot about their sovereignty. They care a lot about economically rebuilding. We do think that there is a pathway there, but it really does require a firm and verifiable commitment that they don’t rebuild that nuclear program,” Vance said.

Trump stressed in his remarks Monday that his bottom-line demand that Iran not possess a nuclear weapon.

“We’re not going to allow Iran ever to have a nuclear weapon, and they understand that. They’ve understood that and they’ve said it even recently,” Trump said.

“If we allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, this country could never function in the same way. The whole world would be a different place,” he said.

He insisted that the operation was not actually a war because “we’ve done very little fighting” recently, after the sweeping US and Israeli strikes that began in late February wrapped up months ago.

“We wiped out their leaders — first level of leaders, the second level of leaders, and they’ve asked us, please stop doing that, and we will,” Trump further claimed.

‘Very intensive’ negotiations

Echoing Vance, two regional officials who spoke to the Associated Press said diplomatic efforts have made progress, with Qatari mediators holding two rounds of talks last week with Iranian officials.

The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing what they said were classified briefings they had received from American, and in one case Israeli, officials.

A diplomat familiar with the negotiations told The Times of Israel that a delegation of Qatari mediators arrived in Tehran during the evening to resume talks with Iranian officials about a potential agreement. The deal under discussion would see the swift reopening of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran in exchange for sanctions relief from the US, followed by comprehensive talks on Tehran’s nuclear program, the diplomat said.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi confirmed that “intensive” talks with Washington were taking place via mediators.

“Consultations through mediators are very intensive. We have presented our conditions and proposals, and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington,” Araghchi said in comments carried by state media outlet IRNA.

Quoting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, state media in Iran reported that supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei gave “certain authorities” to the elected government in talks with the US and mediators.

Iran seeks “to solve the problem with dialogue,” Pezeshkian said, according to the IRNA news agency.

Iran’s foreign ministry said it was considering a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the US agrees to its conditions, having previously proposed a one-week timeline.

“The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran’s good-faith approach. We have stated that, if Iran’s demands are met, it would be possible to restore security to the Strait of Hormuz and resume the negotiating process within a short period,” said foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei, adding that the “exchange of messages is still ongoing” via mediators.

Baghaei said the plan Iran had submitted in September to end the war remained the focus of discussions, but he confirmed comments attributed to Araghchi on Saturday that the proposal could be shortened.

“The basis of dialogue and talks between Iran and the US via mediators is still Iran’s seven-step proposal, which is now condensed, making it possible to implement it within two days,” he said.

Trump in September rejected the seven-step proposal, which called for the US to end its blockade on Iranian ports, Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz waterway, a US waiver on Iranian oil sales, the cancellation of new sanctions on Iran and then talks on other issues.

Baghaei reiterated that condensing the plan would not change Iran’s underlying stance that a return to talks on the country’s nuclear program could only happen after it verified that all its conditions were met.

Asked whether the possibility of transferring Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile to another country was raised in the talks, and whether Iran might agree to that, he said no.

Netanyahu said pushing for renewed strikes
Amid the diplomatic efforts, two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter told the Associated Press that Netanyahu was pushing for another wave of strikes on Iran after the US elections on Tuesday.

Netanyahu pressed for strikes during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.

Other US allies in the Middle East are warning against more strikes, saying it would destabilize the region and could lead Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen to step up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, a third regional official said. Iran-backed militias in Iraq could also get involved.

That official, and the person familiar with the Netanyahu-Trump call, were not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.

A resumption of the conflict with Iran could potentially help Netanyahu form an emergency government after he and his allies lost their Knesset majority in last week’s elections. Netanyahu also pushed for renewed strikes before the vote as he sought to highlight his security credentials to a public deeply scarred by Hamas’s October 7, 2023, terror onslaught.

The Israeli government did not immediately comment. The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Trump’s discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call, which the premier’s office also not has commented on.

text:
Keeping sea lanes open is nothing more than an excuse Washington uses to drag South Korea and Japan into its strategy of containing China.

That argument simply doesn't hold up. Even in the event of a military conflict over Taiwan, maritime routes between China and Northeast Asia would not be limited to a single corridor. Routes east of Taiwan and even the Arctic shipping routes offer alternative options.

The real issue is geopolitics.

Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and the Philippines form the key strategic positions along the US First Island Chain. Through this chain, Washington has sought to contain China within the Western Pacific.

But as China's military capabilities have grown, the United States has increasingly shifted its strategic focus toward the Second Island Chain, leaving its allies on the front line.

The strategy is quite simple: let its allies confront China directly and absorb the initial military pressure, weaken China's military capabilities, and then have US forces enter the decisive battle.

But this strategy is becoming increasingly unrealistic.

China has already embarked on a major military transformation toward unmanned warfare. In a future conflict, countries along the First Island Chain could face massive waves of hypersonic missiles, drones, unmanned surface vessels, robotic ground combat systems, and a North Korean military that has gained combat experience and undergone extensive modernization.

One of the most striking ironies is that the "Hellscape" warfare concept proposed by Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, to deter China has also become an important reference point in China's military thinking.

At its core is the idea of converting industrial capacity into military power: deploying large numbers of unmanned combat systems to impose attrition on an adversary while minimizing human losses. In other words, using steel to save lives.

If South Korea gets involved in a full-scale war against China, regardless of the eventual outcome, the price could be catastrophic. The country itself could be reduced to a wasteland.

I believe President Lee Jae-myung understands this danger.

His insistence on regaining wartime operational control during his term is not simply about military sovereignty. It is about ensuring that South Korea retains control over its own national destiny.

He understands the stakes.

He does not want South Korea to become a sacrificial pawn on America's geopolitical chessboard.

text:
The Left didn’t abandon the Jews. It never stood with them.
As Left-wing parties nominate open supporters of Hamas, Jewish leftists are bemoaning an abandonment that was never a real relationship.
DANIEL GREENFIELD
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (center) meeting with U.S. President Barack Obama in 2013, with Israeli President Shimon Peres behind him (photo: Pete Souza/Wikipedia)📷

This is a guest essay written by Daniel Greenfield, a Shillman Journalism Fellow at the David Horowitz Freedom Center.

The nomination of open Hamas supporters by the Democratic Party has led to another round of American Jewish leftists bemoaning their abandonment by the party and the movement, despite the time they marched with Martin Luther King Jr.

But the Democratic Party didn’t abandon the Jews. It never stood with them in the first place.

When was the Democratic Party ever friendly to Jews? Was it the antisemitism of New Deal litigation that targeted Jews in the Schechter chicken case? Was it when Franklin D. Roosevelt told Joseph Stalin that he might give the Saudi regime “the six million Jews in the United States,” after watching six million Jews die in Europe? Was it when Harry S. Truman slapped an arms embargo on Israel as it fought for independence, and later told his biographer that “there’s never been a Jew inside the house”?

Even the brief honeymoon after the Holocaust, when the Democrats at least pretended to deplore public displays of antisemitism, came quickly to an end with the degeneration of the civil rights movement, championed earnestly by Jewish leftists, into black militant groups.

By the end of the 1960s, antisemitic race riots had torn apart entire communities, and antisemitic statements by Black leaders were becoming a routine part of life that the Democratic Party learned to accept. Some Jewish leftist groups protested, mostly to no avail. They held civil rights gatherings to reboot the mostly mythical black-Jewish alliance, and the Anti-Defamation League issued surveys documenting clear patterns of antisemitism and suggested teaching Black people more about the Holocaust.

Over the next half century, a line of openly antisemitic hatemongers — including Jesse Jackson, Louis Farrakhan, and Al Sharpton — was added to the pantheon of Black leaders and became power players in the Democratic Party. Most Jewish Democrats learned to live with it and, after issuing occasional statements, to shut up about it.

Despite having called New York City “Hymietown” and supporting Islamic terrorists, Jesse Jackson finished third in the 1984 Democratic presidential primaries and second in 1988. After the Crown Heights Pogrom, Al Sharpton ran for the presidential nomination, got an MSNBC show, and became a kingmaker in the Democratic Party. This had nothing to do with “Israel,” “Zionism,” or anything except straightforward racism.

On the Israel side, White Democrats from Adlai Stevenson to Jimmy Carter became quite comfortable attacking Jews in antisemitic language, with even less response from Jewish Democrats. For the most part, though, Democrats paid lip service to condemning antisemitism, just not when it came from prominent members of their own party. After the brief honeymoon under John F. Kennedy and Lyndon B. Johnson, they also paid lip service to supporting Israel while undermining it when in office.

Barack Obama felt empowered to engineer a public break with pro-Israel groups. Yet he was pursuing the same underlying foreign policy as Jimmy Carter and Bill Clinton; he was simply more strategically confrontational about picking fights with Jews and Israel to fracture the party.

The events of October 7th were similarly used to help engineer a break that was already underway, following prior clashes over the antisemitic leadership of the Women’s March and the elevation of Black Lives Matter, along with its antisemitism, to morally unchallenged status in the party’s activist coalition.

Universities had long since ceded student government and entire departments to anti-Israel groups and terrorist supporters. The atrocities of October 7th and the Israeli campaign against Hamas enabled a social media contagion and an activist mobilization that were already underway.

Many Jewish Democrats, at least those who don’t mouth the same apologetics blaming Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and AIPAC, feel betrayed and abandoned. But there was never any actual relationship there, just an affair that eventually gave way to a public declaration of adultery.

The longstanding relationship between the Jews and the Democrats was a mostly one-sided affair in which Jews voted for Democrats, donated to them, and readjusted their religion to echo whatever flavor of leftist politics the party was subscribing to at the moment. In exchange, Jews were able to hold political office and staff the party and its leftist allies.

But, much like the FDR and Truman administrations, leftist Jews were convinced that the party was not antisemitic because it included Jews, without ever looking at the bottom line. This approach was good for the careers and social status of some leftist Jews, who could afford to move out of urban neighborhoods to the suburbs and swallow public insults from minority leaders as unimportant to the bigger picture of their values and the cause.

The latest twist requires them to readapt not only to the congressional nominations of the likes of Dariazila Avila Chevalier in New York, who attended a celebration of October 7th after the attacks, and Melat Kiros in Colorado, who denied that a Muslim terrorist who set elderly Jews on fire, including a Holocaust survivor, hated Jews, but also to the Democratic Party welcoming them to its ranks.

It’s shocking, but not really a new trend. Democrats dropped even pro forma condemnations of antisemitism from their own side back in the late 1990s. By the time the picture of Obama posing with Louis Farrakhan came out, everyone just ignored it. What is different this time is that Democratic Party antisemitism isn’t just something leftist Jews can ignore.

A purge is moving through the movement, its societal and professional enclaves, and the party — shunning, demonizing and actively pushing Jews out. There’s no retreating from Brownsville to Westchester, because “Brownsville” is now everywhere. It’s in suburban neighborhoods, in private schools, on college campuses, and among medical associations and law firms. It determines who gets roommates, book contracts, and the ability to live the upper-middle-class lifestyle that so many leftist Jews had long since come to take for granted.

Some try to adapt. Like their former brethren in the USSR, they measure exactly how much to denounce, condemning Netanyahu, Zionism, and Israel, and even praising the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine or Hamas. Others are caught in a “fight or flight” reaction after the October 7th attacks.

But the good news for them is that the Jews aren’t special. Or they’re only so special.

Jews have long been canaries in the coal mine, and an obsession with them tends to mark the arrival of a broader and bloodier extremism. Life may not be as pleasant in the Park Slope Coop or at Columbia University, but the radical movements doing this are not well disposed to the continued existence of the upper middle class, or of America itself.

The Jews may face the threat of being the first up against the wall, whether from the Democratic Socialists of America’s Marxist and Communist entryists now busily hollowing out the Democratic Party, or from the Islamists working both sides of the aisle. But history tells us they will not be the last.

The moment does not call for more paroxysms of neuroticism, or for plays like “Birthright” and “The Zionists,” which completely fail to deal with what is going on. It calls for an honest reckoning with the history of the Democratic Party and the Jews, abandoning the old myths of solidarity, and dealing with the cold realities of self-preservation and the preservation of an open American society.

To paraphrase a Marxist truism, “The issue isn’t the Jews. The issue is the revolution.”

The Jews were a useful stand-in for capitalism for Karl Marx and other prominent socialists. The USSR and its Communist allies were purging Jews long before the old class hatred was internationalized into the third-world liberationism that now calls for the destruction of Israel.

The growing influence of leftism in the Democratic Party was bound to make it more antisemitic. Combine that with the tribal hatreds of minority and third-world activists, and the Democrats look less like the party of JFK and more like the United Nations and its obsessive scapegoating.

Everyone, including many Jewish leftists, could see it coming, but they chose to stand with a movement that was bound to grow in its hatred for them the closer it came to its goals. The signs had been there since the 1960s and 1970s. Now it’s becoming impossible not to see them.

The “right side of history” is the pursuit of an extremist world order with no room for the Jews.

Jewish Democrats can allow the stable of leftist groups like the Jewish Democratic Council of America, the Nexus Project, J Street, and the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, created to trick them into adopting anti-Israel positions, to guide them into accepting the current horrors as the justifiable new normal. They can align with openly anti-Israel leftist groups like J Street, Jewish Voice for Peace, T’ruah, or Bend the Arc in the hope that it will save their social status and their skin. Or they can have some dignity and fight back.

That will require dealing with some ugly realities. Antisemitism in their party isn’t emerging out of thin air. It’s due to the influence of extremist movements originating within a leftist ideology that dates back centuries. Class warfare invariably turns antisemitic, and a hierarchy of identity politics doesn’t offer “solidarity,” as anti-Israel leftists insist; it unites tribal groups around hatred of Jews.

The Democratic Party didn’t abandon the Jews. Leftist Jews abandoned themselves by accepting antisemitism from the party, refusing to hold it accountable, lowering their expectations, and refocusing around general social justice while ignoring their interests and even their survival.

If they want things to change, that is where it starts.

text:
At what point do the negatives of Deion Sanders’ tenure at Colorado outweigh the positives?

Four seasons in, we’re looking at a 19–26 record, embarrassing in-game mismanagement, one of the most undisciplined teams in college football, and increasingly ridiculous press conferences filled with failed gotcha moments and confrontations with reporters.

And in 2027, Deion Sanders will collect $11 MILLION.

For what, exactly?

He doesn’t travel to recruit. He doesn’t call offensive or defensive plays. His most visible contributions on Saturdays seem limited to motivational speeches, sideline theatrics, and looking bewildered when things inevitably go wrong.

But perhaps the most embarrassing part of this entire experiment isn’t even happening on the football field.

It’s Uncle Neely and the propaganda circus surrounding this program.

Christopher “Uncle Neely” Neely has enjoyed extraordinary access to Colorado football while operating what increasingly resembles a personal public relations campaign for Deion Sanders.

Every embarrassing loss needs an excuse. Every legitimate criticism gets dismissed as hate. Every question about accountability turns into another lecture about how grateful Colorado fans should be that Coach Prime decided to come to Boulder.

That’s not objective football analysis. That’s propaganda.

And the $50,000 controversy perfectly illustrates the problem. Neely publicly suggested Sanders had offered critics money to stop mentioning him, creating a national controversy that Sanders later had to explain away as a joke.

Why does someone with this level of access continue to generate distractions for a struggling football program?

The uncomfortable question is whether Colorado has allowed the line between legitimate media coverage and a coach’s personal promotional operation to become completely blurred.

Meanwhile, fans are constantly reminded of the financial miracle Deion supposedly brought to Boulder.

Let’s examine that.

Colorado’s football ticket revenue dropped from $31.2 million in FY2024 to $24 million in FY2025. The athletic department relied on $43.5 million in university support and student fees in FY2025 and projected a $27 million deficit for FY2026.

And while the Boulder Chamber estimated $146.5 million in regional economic activity from CU football in 2024, that figure isn’t university profit or money deposited directly into the city’s coffers.

Boulder’s own finance department acknowledged that the initial Prime Effect wasn’t enough to materially offset the city’s broader sales-tax stagnation.

Colorado was a major research university long before Deion Sanders arrived. Boulder was a thriving college town long before anyone started selling Coach Prime merchandise.

Nobody disputes that Sanders brought publicity, excitement, a Heisman Trophy winner, and a nine-win season.

But publicity isn’t a substitute for coaching. Economic-impact estimates aren’t a substitute for financial accountability. And a personal hype machine isn’t a substitute for building a disciplined, sustainable football program.

At some point, the university needs to stop evaluating Deion Sanders as a celebrity attraction and start evaluating him as an $11 million football coach.

The results, the discipline, the recruiting approach, the embarrassing media circus, and the refusal to acknowledge obvious shortcomings all deserve scrutiny.

Colorado football should belong to the university, its players, its alumni, and its fans. Not to Deion Sanders, Uncle Neely, or an army of people whose primary interest appears to be protecting a brand.

The publicity was great. The experiment has run its course.

Rip the fucking Band-Aid off and go get Jason Eck.

Colorado needs a football coach, not an $11 million celebrity appearance surrounded by a propaganda department.

text:
LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM

THE EDUCATION OF A STATESMAN AND THE TRAGEDY OF BOLA TINUBU

Why character, intellectual discipline and the principles of honourable leadership matter more than political cunning.

By Kio Amachree
President, Worldview International
Stockholm, Sweden | 3 November 2026

There is a profound difference between a man who has been educated to lead and a man who has merely learned how to acquire power. Nigeria is today paying a terrible price for that distinction.

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has spent much of his political life cultivating the reputation of a master strategist, a political kingmaker, a man who understands the streets and knows how to manipulate the machinery of power. His admirers call him a political genius. I see something rather different: a politician whose remarkable ability to acquire and retain influence has not translated into the intellectual leadership, moral authority or public service that Nigeria so desperately requires.

The tragedy is not simply that Tinubu has failed to live up to the expectations of the presidency. It is that his style of leadership appears to confuse the possession of power with the possession of wisdom, political survival with achievement, and personal influence with national progress.

Nigeria deserves considerably better.

WHAT ETON COLLEGE TAUGHT ME ABOUT LEADERSHIP

I was educated at Eton College in England, one of the world’s oldest and most distinguished schools. Founded in 1440 by King Henry VI, Eton has educated generations of British statesmen, diplomats, scholars, soldiers, entrepreneurs and public servants.

Twenty British prime ministers have been educated at Eton, an extraordinary record for a single school. Among them are Robert Walpole, widely regarded as Britain’s first prime minister, the Duke of Wellington, William Gladstone, Harold Macmillan, David Cameron and Boris Johnson.

But Eton’s distinction is not simply the number of powerful men who have passed through its classrooms.

What mattered to me was the education itself.

We were taught that privilege carried responsibility, that honour was not something to be proclaimed but something to be demonstrated through conduct, and that a man’s reputation should rest upon his integrity rather than his possessions.

We learned that there was a difference between right and wrong, between service and self-interest, between leadership and exploitation.

We were expected to understand that character mattered.

An honourable man does not regard the suffering of others as an opportunity for personal advancement. He does not use public office to enrich his friends while the people he governs struggle to survive. He does not confuse the national treasury with the resources of his political organisation.

Above all, he understands that leadership imposes obligations.

A leader is expected to protect the vulnerable, uphold the law, defend the institutions of the state and leave society stronger than he found it.

These principles are not the exclusive property of Eton or any other institution. Nor does an Eton education guarantee virtue. Some of its graduates have fallen far short of the standards they were taught.

But the principles themselves remain essential.

The purpose of education is not merely to produce a clever man. It is to help produce a responsible one.

THE UNIVERSITY OF PENNSYLVANIA AND THE EDUCATION OF AMBITION

After Eton, I attended the University of Pennsylvania, one of America’s great Ivy League institutions and home to the Wharton School, established in 1881 as the world’s first collegiate business school.

Penn has produced an extraordinary number of successful entrepreneurs, financiers, innovators and public figures.

Donald Trump, the sitting president of the United States, graduated from Wharton in 1968. Elon Musk, one of the wealthiest entrepreneurs in modern history, graduated from the University of Pennsylvania with degrees in economics and physics.

The university’s alumni include influential figures in international finance, technology, industry and public administration.

Wharton has consistently been recognised as one of the world’s leading business schools, and its graduates have helped build and manage some of the world’s most important enterprises.

What distinguishes a serious business education is not simply the pursuit of wealth.

It is the development of analytical discipline, the capacity to evaluate evidence, the ability to understand complicated economic systems and the intellectual confidence to make difficult decisions.

At its best, such an education encourages innovation, initiative, hard work and accountability.

It teaches that ambition without competence is dangerous and that success without responsibility is incomplete.

I do not suggest that every Penn graduate possesses these qualities. The careers of famous alumni demonstrate that educational achievement and moral character are not necessarily the same thing.

But I do insist that intellectual preparation matters, particularly when a man assumes responsibility for the lives and livelihoods of more than 200 million people.

A presidency is not a political reward. It is an immense administrative, economic, constitutional and moral responsibility.

And no amount of political cunning can substitute for the ability to discharge it.

THE EDUCATIONAL QUESTIONS SURROUNDING BOLA TINUBU

It is against this background that I consider the extraordinary controversy surrounding President Tinubu’s educational history.

Tinubu has maintained that he graduated from Chicago State University in 1979. The university has confirmed that he attended and graduated.

That fact must be acknowledged.

But it does not dispose of the wider controversy concerning the documents submitted in his name, discrepancies in his educational history and the questions raised during litigation over his academic records.

The public dispute has never been simply whether Tinubu attended a university. It has concerned the reliability of particular documents, the explanations offered for inconsistencies and the standards of transparency expected of a president.

These matters should not be dismissed as irrelevant technicalities.

A nation’s president should be able to present a coherent, independently verifiable account of his education and personal history without years of litigation, political controversy and public confusion.

Education is supposed to equip a person with the confidence to confront questions through evidence and reason.

The presidency should not be an institution where legitimate scrutiny is treated as an insult.

But I want to make an even more important point.

Even if every dispute over Tinubu’s academic history were resolved in his favour, the question of his fitness for leadership would remain.

A university certificate does not establish moral character. Nor does it prove that its holder possesses the judgment required to govern a nation.

The true examination is taking place every day in Nigeria.

And in my judgment, Tinubu is failing it.

THE STREET IS NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR STATESMANSHIP

Tinubu’s supporters frequently celebrate his political streetcraft.

They speak admiringly of his ability to construct alliances, reward loyalty, neutralise opponents and dominate political structures.

But these are the skills of acquiring power, not necessarily the skills of governing well.

The distinction is fundamental.

A political operator asks how he can retain control. A statesman asks how he can improve the country.

A political operator measures success by the loyalty of those around him. A statesman measures success by the security, prosperity and dignity of ordinary citizens.

A political operator builds networks of dependence. A statesman builds institutions capable of functioning without him.

Nigeria has had more than enough political operators.

What it needs is statesmanship.

I have nothing against the streets. Indeed, some of history’s greatest leaders emerged from poverty and received little formal education. They became remarkable because they possessed integrity, intelligence, courage and a profound understanding of human responsibility.

Nor do I believe that a noble family background automatically produces a noble character.

Nobility is ultimately a matter of conduct.

My criticism of Tinubu is not that he lacks an Eton education, a Wharton degree or an aristocratic upbringing. It is that his conduct in office, in my assessment, demonstrates too little of the ethical discipline that any serious education, whether acquired in a classroom or through life, should cultivate.

Political cunning may win elections.

It cannot build a modern nation.

A COUNTRY LEFT TO THE WOLVES

Look at Nigeria today.

Millions of Nigerians struggle with the cost of food, transportation, housing and basic necessities. Insecurity continues to devastate communities. Kidnapping and violent crime have left families living in fear. Public institutions remain weakened by corruption, patronage and political interference.

Yet the political class continues to enjoy privileges that ordinary citizens can scarcely imagine.

There is something profoundly offensive about a government that demands sacrifice from the poor while failing to demonstrate comparable restraint among those who exercise power.

The Nigerian presidency should be the first institution to demonstrate financial discipline, transparency and respect for public resources.

Instead, Tinubu’s administration has repeatedly attracted controversy over government expenditure, political appointments, public procurement and the relationship between political influence and commercial advantage.

Consider the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway.

The scale of the project, the procurement arrangements, the involvement of Hitech Construction and the political connections surrounding its ownership have raised legitimate questions that deserve transparent, documented answers.

A responsible administration should welcome scrutiny of contracts involving enormous sums of public money.

It should publish the relevant figures, explain the procurement decisions and establish beyond reasonable doubt that the public interest is being protected.

That is how accountable government behaves.

The issue is not whether Nigeria needs modern infrastructure. Of course it does.

The issue is whether infrastructure development is being conducted with the transparency, competitive discipline and independence expected in a functioning democracy.

The people are entitled to know whose interests their government is serving.

They should never be expected to surrender that right because a president regards himself as a political master strategist.

THE MORAL FAILURE OF LEADERSHIP

There is a tendency in Nigerian politics to admire wealth without asking how it was acquired, to celebrate power without examining how it is exercised, and to confuse political longevity with public achievement.

This is one of the most destructive habits in our national life.

A politician becomes wealthy, surrounds himself with loyalists, distributes favours and is suddenly described as a great leader.

But where are the schools?

Where are the hospitals?

Where is the electricity?

Where is the security?

Where is the functioning justice system?

Where is the evidence that ordinary citizens have benefited proportionately from the enormous resources controlled in their name?

These are the questions by which leadership should be judged.

Not the number of private aircraft in a political circle. Not the size of the presidential entourage. Not the enthusiasm of paid supporters. Not the ability to dominate a political party.

The measure of government is the condition of the governed.

A president who cannot provide security, maintain confidence in public institutions and establish a credible path towards prosperity cannot reasonably expect to be celebrated simply because he has mastered the mechanics of political survival.

Nigeria is not a private estate.

Its citizens are not tenants of the president.

And its national resources are not the property of whichever political organisation happens to control Abuja.

THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A RULER AND A SERVANT OF THE PEOPLE

At Eton, I learned that public service should be regarded as an obligation rather than an opportunity for personal enrichment.

At the University of Pennsylvania, I encountered an intellectual environment in which ambition was expected to be accompanied by preparation, competence and the ability to defend one’s ideas.

These lessons have stayed with me throughout my life.

They are also why I find the present condition of Nigerian leadership so deeply troubling.

A serious president should surround himself with independent minds, not merely obedient followers. He should welcome criticism rather than regard dissent as disloyalty. He should understand that the law exists to restrain power, not to serve it.

He should be capable of admitting mistakes.

Most importantly, he should recognise that the people of Nigeria are not there to serve him. He is there to serve them.

What I see under Tinubu is a political culture in which loyalty too often appears more valuable than competence, personal connections more influential than institutional safeguards, and the preservation of political power more urgent than the protection of ordinary citizens.

That is not the foundation of a modern republic.

It is the foundation of a patronage system.

And patronage systems ultimately impoverish the societies they are supposed to govern.

NIGERIA DOES NOT NEED ANOTHER POLITICAL GODFATHER

Nigeria has some of the finest minds in the world.

Our universities, despite decades of neglect, have produced outstanding scientists, physicians, lawyers, economists, engineers and scholars.

Nigerians occupy important positions in international finance, medicine, technology, academia and public administration.

Our people have demonstrated that they can compete successfully in almost every serious intellectual and professional environment.

Yet the country itself remains trapped in a political system that too often rewards connections over qualifications, obedience over independent judgment and political manoeuvring over genuine achievement.

This is an indictment of the system, not of the Nigerian people.

Imagine what Nigeria could become if the intellectual talent of its citizens were matched by a government committed to merit, accountability and the rule of law.

Imagine a presidency that regarded education as an instrument of national development rather than a subject of political controversy.

Imagine a government that measured its success not by the fortunes of those close to power but by the opportunities available to a child born in a poor household in Kano, Port Harcourt, Maiduguri or Lagos.

That is the Nigeria we should be building.

Not a country where political godfathers decide who prospers, where public contracts generate endless suspicion, and where citizens are expected to applaud the powerful while enduring extraordinary hardship.

THE FINAL EXAMINATION

Bola Tinubu may have spent decades learning how to survive in Nigerian politics.

But survival is not statesmanship.

He may have mastered the art of assembling political coalitions, rewarding allies and defeating opponents.

But none of these accomplishments establishes that he possesses the moral imagination or administrative competence required to transform Nigeria.

His Chicago State University degree is a matter of institutional record. His performance as president is a matter for the Nigerian people to judge.

And that is the examination that matters most.

Eton College has educated twenty British prime ministers. The University of Pennsylvania has educated a sitting American president, some of the world’s most successful entrepreneurs and generations of leaders in business and public life.

Their records remind us of the importance of intellectual preparation, ambition and institutional excellence.

But their greatest lesson is not that a prestigious education makes a person superior.

It is that opportunity creates responsibility, that achievement must be accompanied by character, and that the exercise of power should be governed by principles greater than personal advantage.

I would rather see Nigeria governed by an honest man educated in a village school than by a highly credentialed man who treats the country as his private possession.

I would rather have a president of modest origins who understands justice than a wealthy political operator who cannot distinguish between the interests of his associates and the interests of the nation.

Nigeria does not need a president who can outmanoeuvre everyone around him.

It needs a president who can govern.

A president who understands economics beyond political slogans, security beyond official motorcades, education beyond certificates, and leadership beyond the distribution of favours.

A president who understands that the first duty of government is to protect the people, not to leave them to the wolves while those in power enjoy the comforts of office.

Tinubu’s greatest failure, in my assessment, is not a question of where he went to school.

It is what he has failed to demonstrate that he learned.

The tragedy of Nigeria is that a nation overflowing with intelligence, ambition and talent has entrusted its future to a political establishment that has shown itself far more accomplished at acquiring power than at exercising it honourably.

The country deserves a different standard.

Education without character is insufficient. Ambition without integrity is dangerous. Power without accountability is an invitation to abuse.

And a presidency without a genuine commitment to the welfare of its people is not leadership.

It is merely the occupation of an office.

Nigeria has endured far too much of that already.

Kio Amachree
President, Worldview International

Stockholm, Sweden

text:
After considerable thought, I have resigned my membership of Reform UK and decided to rejoin the Conservative Party.

Over recent months, I have become increasingly frustrated with Reform's embrace of left-wing economic policies, growing social conservatism, and a concerning shift towards nationalism, particularly its support for protectionist measures such as tariffs.

I have also become disillusioned with the apparent lack of tolerance for internal criticism. Having previously received ridicule from Reform supporters for defending the principle that being gay or transgender should never be a crime, I have increasingly questioned whether my commitment to individual liberty is shared by those around me.

Ultimately, my political ideology has not changed. I remain committed to individual liberty, free-market economics, limited government, and personal responsibility. Rather, I believe Reform UK has moved away from the principles that initially attracted me to the party.

Whilst I recognise that the Conservatives are far from perfect, I believe they offer greater opportunities for open debate, constructive criticism, and the advancement of my political beliefs.

@Conservatives

text:
Hermes merged 190 PRs on November 2

The ones worth knowing:

- The gateway no longer freezes every minute for memory trims, and gateway and serve stop hoarding free memory across ~160 malloc arenas
- Grok Bot and OpenBot users can move to Hermes from setup, and hermes migrate <agent> installs the importer for you
- Each Desktop terminal tab now owns its own gateway, and SSH gateways list every profile at launch
- Old phone app chats now continue in Desktop instead of opening read only
- Desktop renders mermaid diagrams with Pele instead of mermaid.js, so they draw faster
- A transient 401 on a valid Nous agent key no longer kills your turn in about 1.5 seconds
- The local web server (Webapp, dashboard, serve) now trusts only the bound loopback origin for CORS and WebSockets
- MCP servers started for a profile use that profile's home, and recovered MCP servers show up in new sessions without /reload-mcp
- Slack gets an opt in thread_followup_silence setting for unaddressed thread replies
- A killed update no longer leaves lock files behind that block the next update
- Background /bg results and async delegation completions now reliably reach the right chat
- Over 100 plugin catalog adds and bumps, including the Fortytwo model provider, Upstash Box terminal backend and bubblewrap sandboxed file tools

“These glasses allow operators to see things ordinary personnel cannot,” explained a Pentagon spokesman, examining his fingers through the lenses. “For example, I can clearly see that my hand has a hand inside it.”

The breakthrough followed an eighteen-month search for technology capable of identifying threats behind walls. After reviewing proposals from fourteen defense contractors, officials selected a supplier whose qualifications included a small illustration of a boy looking through another boy’s arm.

“The demonstration was compelling,” said the procurement director. “There were bones.”

Under the fictional deployment plan, the team would approach a hostile compound under cover of darkness, activate the glasses by putting them on, and identify enemy positions through reinforced concrete. During testing, however, operators reported difficulty seeing through the compound, their briefing folders, or the packaging the glasses arrived in.

The manufacturer attributed these limitations to improper expectations.

“The original advertisement clearly says ‘AMAZING X-RAY EFFECT,’” a company representative explained. “At no point did we promise the United States would successfully invade anything.”

Pentagon officials defended the purchase, noting that the glasses require no batteries, emit no detectable electronic signature, and can be replaced by mailing a coupon to a post office box that has been closed since 1973.

A classified field evaluation obtained for this entirely fictional report described the first operational trial. The point man studied a concrete wall for several minutes before announcing that he could detect a faint outline of his own eyelashes. Command immediately requested coordinates.

In a final procurement update, officials confirmed that the Sea-Monkeys have arrived.

text:
Cerca Trova Restaurant Group Holdings, Inc. (dba Out West Restaurant Group), a San Diego, CA-based franchisee and operator of Outback Steakhouse restaurants, filed for Chapter 11 protection on Nov. 2 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware.

The company attributes its distress to debt it took on to finance expansion, compounded by declining guest traffic, commodity inflation and rising labor costs driven largely by successive minimum wage increases in California. After revenue fell approximately 35% in fiscal 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic, the debtors did not repay or refinance their prepetition credit facility at its April 2022 maturity. They have since operated under forbearance agreements, with interest accruing at the default rate and being capitalized into the loan balance. Covenant EBITDA fell from approximately $22.1 million in fiscal 2023 to approximately $8.4 million in fiscal 2025 and approximately $6.3 million for the twelve months ended Aug. 23, 2026, while fiscal 2025 interest expense of approximately $45.9 million was more than five times that year's covenant EBITDA. The debtors missed their $15.0 million minimum EBITDA covenant during 2025, and in April 2026 the prepetition agent, Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group, delivered a notice of events of default. With the revolver fully drawn, a $1.6 million wage-and-hour class settlement payment coming due and the forbearance period expiring on Dec. 27, 2026, the debtors say they cannot meet these obligations without a sale.

The filing aims to facilitate a court-supervised, going-concern sale of substantially all of the debtors' restaurant assets, with franchisor Outback Steakhouse of Florida, LLC, a subsidiary of Bloomin' Brands, Inc., serving as stalking horse bidder. The stalking horse APA provides for a $26.3 million cash price, the assumption of certain liabilities and the franchisor's release of approximately $13.9 million in deferred royalties, marketing fees and other obligations, subject to higher or otherwise better offers. The proposed bid deadline is Dec. 8 and the proposed sale hearing is Dec. 15. The franchisor would also provide a revolving DIP facility of up to $5.5 million, which bears no interest and would prime the prepetition lenders' liens with their consent. Prepetition secured obligations total approximately $319.9 million, including approximately $190.9 million in accrued and capitalized interest, fees and other obligations. They far exceed the stalking horse cash price, and the debtors have no material unencumbered assets.

Cerca Trova Restaurant Group Holdings, Inc. reports $0 to $50 thousand in assets and $100 million to $500 million in liabilities. The filing indicates that no funds will be available for distribution to unsecured creditors after administrative expenses are paid. The case number is 26-11749.

🍾🇺🇸Police trip to Florida🇺🇸🍾

The council recently hotly debated whether to allow eight police leaders to go on a trip to Florida last week to honor an officer’s heroism in responding to the Annunciation Catholic Church shootings.
The International Association of Chiefs of Police nominated Inspector Ryan Kelly for Police Officer of the Year for his unblinking, “exceptional valor” in responding to the mass shooting.
The Minneapolis Police Foundation offered to pay Kelly’s way with a $16,000 donation, and the police department initially proposed that the city spend another nearly $14,000 so eight more officers could go along to the Orlando event.
Some council members had a problem with paying for a bunch of top cops to go along for the trip, given the police department’s budget-busting ways and the fact that a lot of the brass would be gone for a week.
This led to debate, with more progressive council members blasting MPD for its over-spending, and more moderate members saying that’s a separate issue.
In her newsletter to constituents, Council Member Elizabeth Shaffer said: “I believe that when we lift up the department in moments like these, we improve morale and we reinforce the kind of department we want MPD to be.”
In the end, the foundation came up with more money to cover the whole amount for all the officers to go to the event, as well as the Major Cities Chiefs Association Conference preceding it.

text:
The Lear Jet Crash in Florida.

First my condolences and prayers to the deceased, their families and acquittances.

Two observations.

First, I am dismayed by the number of internet experts that offered opinions about what happened, did not happen, what the pilots were doing or should have been doing without any firsthand experience or knowledge of the situation. Anything for likes, I guess.

Second. I was revolted by the number of “Florida People” walking about the crash scene picking up and examining pieces of wreckage and, perhaps, human remains in shorts, t-shirts, flipflops, bare feet while having their smartphones glued to their face observing and recording the death and destruction.

Why?

Most normal people do not get any pleasure and enjoyment from observing and recording scenes of death and destruction, but I guess some do.

I avoid both and do not want to see nor be reminded of them.

NBA 🏀 Golden State Warriors vs. Phoenix Suns (November 3, 5:00 AM)

current polymarket valuation:

Golden State Warriors - 57¢
Phoenix Suns - 44¢

This marks the second head-to-head matchup between the two teams in ten days. On October 24 in Phoenix, the Suns secured a 131-122 victory; however, the landscape has shifted significantly heading into this rematch in California.
In their first encounter, the Warriors’ loss to the Suns was due entirely to the absence of key veterans, as both Stephen Curry and Draymond Green sat out. This past Sunday, Steve Kerr opted to rest Curry and Green once again during the game against the Clippers, ensuring they would be fresh for this specific matchup. Notably, even without their stars, Golden State’s reserve-heavy lineup managed to rout the Clippers (124-112), fueled by a 37-point performance from rookie Yaxel Lendeborg and a barrage of 22 three-pointers.

Golden State Warriors strengths:

1. Fresh legs for Stephen Curry and Draymond Green: Both Curry (averaging 29.2 points per game) and Green (7.2 assists per game) enjoyed a full rest during the game against the Clippers. Playing at home in the Chase Center, this duo offers maximum tactical versatility, particularly in pick-and-roll situations.
2. The meteoric rise of Yaxel Lendeborg: The Warriors’ rookie is enjoying the season of his life. On Sunday against the Clippers, he recorded 37 points, 6 assists, and 6 three-pointers; in the previous meeting against the Suns, he tallied 26 points and 9 rebounds. 
3. Perimeter firepower: With Butler and Moody sidelined, the Warriors' second unit is delivering elite shooting De'Anthony Melton hit 6 of 8 three-pointers (21 points), while Brandin Podziemski contributed 17 points, 8 rebounds, and 8 assists. The team connected on 22 of 49 attempts from beyond the arc (44.9%) in their last outing.

Golden State Warriors weaknesses and roster Issues:

1. Injury concerns: Jimmy Butler (ACL) and Moses Moody (knee) are out until the winter, and Kristaps Porziņģis is also unavailable.
2. Interior defense struggles: Lacking size at the center position, the Warriors conceded 60 points in the paint during their first matchup against the Suns.
Charles Bassey and Al Horford will need to play physically and commit hard fouls near the rim.

Phoenix Suns strengths:

A Federal jury today found the wealthy securities analyst E. Newbold Smith and three co-defendants not guilty of conspiring to kidnap Mr. Smith's son, an heir to the du Pont family fortune, and "deprogram" him.

The Government had charged that Mr. Smith planned the kidnapping because of his son's involvement with the political extremist Lyndon H. LaRouche Jr., who is now serving a 15-year prison sentence for conspiracy to evade taxes, commit mail fraud and other offenses related to fund raising.

But after deliberating for 12 hours over two days, the eight men and four women on the jury returned verdicts clearing all of the defendants this afternoon. The defendants acknowledged that they discussed a possible abduction but argued that the idea had been rejected without any action taken.

Mr. Smith, who is 66, and his wife, Margaret du Pont Smith, who live outside Philadelphia, assert that their son, Lewis du Pont Smith, 33, is mentally ill and has fallen prey to a cult, as they view the LaRouche movement.

In 1986, a judge in a civil case agreed with the parents that Lewis was mentally ill and was likely to squander his $10 million fortune on Mr. LaRouche's organizations. As a result of that ruling, the son was placed under the control of a financial guardian. He is now trying to have that decision overturned in a Philadelphia court.

Edgar Newbold Smith has spent the last seven years trying to extricate his son, an heir to the Du Pont chemical fortune, from the extremist political organization of Lyndon H. LaRouche Jr.

But Mr. Smith, a securities analyst here, has little to show for his efforts, apart from his son's enmity. And now Mr. Smith is scheduled to stand trial in Alexandria, Va., on Federal charges that he conspired with cult specialists to kidnap his 36-year-old son, Lewis duPont Smith, so the son could be "deprogrammed," or freed from Mr. LaRouche's influence.

The discussions among Mr. Smith and the specialists were revealed to the authorities by a private investigator who had been hired to follow Mr. Smith's son. Eventually the authorities tape recorded 60 hours of conversations. If convicted, Mr. Smith and the three cult specialists could receive sentences ranging from probation to life in prison. The trial begins Monday.

Mr. Smith denies there was a kidnapping plan, but he does not deny that he had considered abduction. "It's just like my son is being held hostage by terrorists in Lebanon, with very much the same set of emotions," Mr. Smith said as he and his wife, Margaret duPont Smith, were interviewed at their home in this affluent Philadelphia suburb.

"When I think of all that's been lost, it's tragic," said Mrs. Smith, who accuses the LaRouche organization of turning her son against his parents, sister, two brothers and childhood friends, not to mention the Du PontChemical Company, which the son, a shareholder, says is run by gangsters. Declared Incompetent

The younger Mr. Smith lives with his wife, Andrea Diano-Smith, in the fashionable Chestnut Hill section of Philadelphia. Both work as fund-raisers for the LaRouche organization. In 1985, after Mr. Smith gave $212,000 to Mr. LaRouche, a Pennsylvania court, at the family's request, declared him incompetent to manage his financial affairs. A Delaware bank was appointed to act as financial guardian of his $10 million inheritance.

The LaRouche organization, based in Leesburg, Va., raises money for political campaigns and publications that promote Mr. LaRouche's theories of international conspiracies and his extremist views on how to fight drug trafficking and revive the economy. Mr. LaRouche is serving a 15-year prison sentence in Minnesota. He and six of his fund-raisers were convicted in 1988 of conspiracy to defraud elderly contributors of $30 million.

Mr. Smith appeared, elegantly dressed, for a recent interview saying he would spend only 30 minutes with a member of the "corrupt media," but he wound up giving a 2 1/2-hour discourse on his family's "humiliating" efforts to control his life. Writing a Book

He also spoke at length about Mr. LaRouche's conspiracy theories, including one that links Queen Elizabeth 2d to the international drug trade. On his family, he said he would tell all in a book he is writing. Its title, he said, would be "Blood Feud: The Story That's Rocking the Richest Family in America."

Civil libertarians say the Smith case raises disturbing questions about the LaRouche organization, some of which have followed it since its founding. Is the group a destructive cult that preys on the elderly and the infirm? Or is it a political party whose zealous adherents sometimes get in legal trouble by soliciting money to publish their unconventional theories?

Civil libertarians are also raising new questions: Is it an expression of mental illness to contribute money to Mr. LaRouche? And should the Government prosecute the elder Mr. Smith for considering, but not committing, a crime? 'Spiral of Thought Control'

Experts on cults are sharply divided in their opinions of the LaRouche organization, and Stefan Presser, legal director of the American Civil Liberties Union in Philadelphia, said civil libertarians are trying to keep an open mind.

Summing up his view of this case, Mr. Presser said: "The father doesn't like what the son is thinking and was considering imposing his own thoughts on the son. The irony is full circle now that the prosecutor is going after the father just for thinking about imposing his thoughts on the son. This is a kind of never-ending spiral of thought control that civil libertarians find intolerable."

Lawrence J. Leiser, the Assistant United States Attorney in Alexandria, Va., who is prosecuting the kidnapping charge, would not discuss the case, but he argued in recent court papers that many of these questions could not be resolved in court.

"The defendants will call their cult experts to say the LaRouche organization was a cult," Mr. Leiser wrote. "The Government will call its experts to say it was nothing more than a political organization. They will call their people to say 'deprogramming' works; we will call ours to say that it is ridiculous to suggest that you can 'deprogram' someone out of their political positions.

"We can listen to testimony that Lewis duPont Smith is incompetent and the defendants' 'purpose' was to save him as a result of that incompetence from an evil and corrupt political organization. The Government can call its experts to show that Lewis duPont Smith is not incompetent." 'Height of Irony'

Mr. Leiser had summarized these thorny issues in an unsuccessful effort to exclude them from the trial and narrow the trial to legal issues surrounding the kidnapping itself.

The elder Mr. Smith's lawyer, John J. E. Markham 2d, said in court papers that it was "the height of irony" for Federal prosecutors to seek such a blanket exclusion because it was the United States Attorney in Alexandria that had prosecuted Mr. LaRouche in the first place.
