Mr. Markham has said in court papers that he will present the elder Mr. Smith as a father who was simply considering ways to rescue a mentally ill son from a criminal group and that he had come to no decision when he was arrested.

Judge Thomas S. Ellis of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia has decided to rule on the relevance of each issue as it comes up in the trial. Accused of Fraud in 1989

Charges similar to those in the 1988 criminal case against LaRouche were made in a 1989 civil suit against the younger Mr. Smith and several of his colleagues in the LaRouche organization. Lydia Baldasar, a 78-year-old widow in Northport, L.I., said in court papers that Mr. Smith and the others had defrauded her of $20,000 in cash and $50,000 in securities by telling her, in meetings, some of which lasted as long as seven hours, that her blue chip stocks were worthless and that the nation's banks and corporations were collapsing.

Ms. Baldasar said she was told that some of her money would be used to prevent the assassination of world leaders. The LaRouche organization settled the case by returning the woman's donation.

The younger Mr. Smith said he and his family had spent more than $1 million on court battles about his mental health. In the 1985 competency case, a state court held lengthy hearings before ruling, on basis of psychiatrists' testimony, that Mr. Smith was mentally ill, incompetent to manage his own financial affairs and prone to falling prey to others.

In his decision, Judge Lawrence Wood said that Mr. Smith had lost more than $100,000 in "ill advised" schemes involving silver mines and walnut trees, and that he had given $212,000 to the LaRouche organization, which, the court said, had "unusual, if not suspect, motives." The court appointed a financial guardian for Mr. Smith's $10 million trust fund and set his annual living allowance at $180,000.

The ruling was upheld in subsequent appeals, and the United States Supreme Court refused to hear the case in 1988. All Plots, No Action

In the current case involving the elder Smith, court papers do not suggest that a kidnapping was planned, only that Mr. Smith had seriously considered the idea and, his lawyer says, rejected it without committing any crime. But in transcripts of the Government's secretly recorded discussions, the consultants sound like characters in a Mickey Spillane mystery.

There is loose talk about a seductress, blackmail, sedative-laced drinks and the use of a motorcycle gang or mercenaries to kidnap the younger Smith and possibly his wife. There is talk about wrapping the unconscious son in a rug and putting him aboard the Smith family's 44-foot yacht for a voyage to a place where "bribery is king" and where the deprogramming would be tried.

Prosecutors say the defendants were ironing out the details of a kidnapping, a claim the elder Mr. Smith's lawyer disputes.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation and a Government informant secretly recorded the discussions, as well as telephone conversations, last summer and early fall. Life Sentence Possible

Whether the evidence proves a criminal kidnapping conspiracy will be up to the jury. If convicted, Mr. Smith, who is 66 years old, and the three other defendants face sentences of up to life in prison.

The other defendants are Galen G. Kelly, 45, of Esopus, N.Y., a specialist in cultic groups; Robert Point, 38, a lawyer from South Amboy, N.J., who has worked on cult cases with Mr. Kelly, and Donald L. Moore, 45, a former deputy sheriff in Loudoun County, Va., where the LaRouche organization has its headquarters.

9 PM Top-of-the-Hour News

President Trump laid out the Republican case one last time today before tomorrow's midterms...: “This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime. The Democratic Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous. slate of candidates in American history. ”
Many polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance of flipping control of both the House and Senate in Tuesday's elections.

Michigan’s Senate race is up for grabs this midterm.
Oakland University political science professor David Dulio says it's been a hard fought and bitter campaign between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers...: “Part of the strategy on the part of El Sayed has been to turn Mike Rogers into Donald Trump, and on the flip side, Mike Rogers and his campaign have tried to make Abdul El Sayed simply an unacceptable choice. ”
The campaign took a turn Sunday when Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens threw her endorsement behind the Republican Rogers.

A federal judge is throwing out a criminal case against two former FBI officials, accusing the Justice Department of political prosecution.: “The two officials were accused of lying to Congress about their involvement in investigations into Hunter Biden, but the judge says prosecutors didn't have enough evidence to show they knowingly made false statements. He also criticized the rushed investigation and questioned why the case was brought just ahead of tomorrow's midterm election. He called it the weaponization of federal law enforcement, adding, quote, I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend I cannot read a calendar. The decision is another setback for the Trump administration's efforts to investigate its political adversaries, Stacy Linn, Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

Senator Chris Murphy continues to recover after he suffered a stroke on Saturday.
A spokesman for the Connecticut Democrat says Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game in Maryland.
Murphy was taken to a local hospital where it was confirmed that he had a stroke. He was then transferred to Johns Hopkins in Baltimore.

Officials continue to investigate yesterday's Lear jet crash in West Palm Beach, Florida that killed all nine people aboard.
The NTSB's Thomas Chapman...: “A transmission from the airplane announced the descent, followed by a mayday call. About 12:48 Eastern, the airplane transmitted. We are in an overspeed condition, descending with the rest unintelligible. ”
Reports say the co-pilot of the private jet was 20-year-old Nathalia Ga-del-ha  , who got her pilot's license in high school, before she got her driver's license.

Weeks after her murder trial for killing her three children ended in a mistrial, Lindsay Clancy was back in a Massachusetts courtroom today.
Her lawyers are arguing the charges should be dismissed, because her postpartum psychosis made her strangle her kids. Prosecutors could seek to retry her or offer a plea deal.

Heavy rain has triggered flash flooding and evacuations in parts of the Southwest...: “Rain fell almost nonstop in Flagstaff, Arizona, overwhelming storm drains. The downpours prompted the closure of several highways in the state. The latest round of rain was expected to continue through today with as much as 4 inches of rain across the region. The city of Flagstaff says that administrative offices and nonessential facilities will be closed today in order to allow emergency staff and employees to respond to flooding incidents. Administrative offices are set to reopen Tuesday, with voting locations expected to operate as normal. Gloria Chapa, Worldwide News Network. ”

The cryptocurrency exchange Binance says its customers have withdrawn 4.7 billion dollars since it reopened yesterday.
The FBI says North Korean hackers stole 6.3 billion dollars from Binance Thursday night.

Is Trump’s MAGA Movement About to Face Its First Major Electoral Setback?

America goes to the polls today for the 2026 Midterm Elections, and the early polling trends are not looking particularly encouraging for Donald Trump and the Republicans. Democrats appear well placed to win control of the House of Representatives, while the Senate race remains more challenging. All eyes are on seven key states: Michigan, Texas, Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa and Alaska. Texas is particularly interesting. Traditionally a Republican stronghold, it is now showing signs of becoming a much tighter contest. Even in conservative states such as Iowa and Kansas, Democrats appear to be making gains. This could suggest that Trump's economic and political message is losing some of its appeal. My feeling is that Democrats have a stronger chance of winning the House, but taking control of the Senate will be the real test. If they manage to win both chambers, Trump's ability to push through legislation and control government spending could face serious challenges, potentially changing the political landscape ahead of the 2028 presidential election. But these elections are about more than Trump's personal popularity. They are also a test of how Americans feel about the economy, the cost of living and his administration's performance. The big question is: are Americans beginning to move away from MAGA politics, or is this simply a temporary wave of anti-Trump sentiment? The results in Texas and Alaska could offer some important clues.

Afshan Bangash

🔑📜✨️Grand Scholarly Abstract

The prophetic truth of the late fifteenth century achieved an extraordinary expression in Sibyllae et Prophetae de Christo Salvatore Vaticinantes, an illuminated manuscript whose pictorial theology extends beyond conventional biblical illustration into the ancient and intricate problem of universal revelation, the antiquity of Messianic knowledge, the survival of sacred testimony among the nations, and the chronological transmission of divine promises from the primordial patriarchs to the manifestation of Jesus Christ. 

Within its illuminated folios, twelve ancient Sibyls, Hebrew prophets, and evangelical witnesses participate in an exceptionally sophisticated construction of sacred history. 

Their respective testimonies are arranged through imposing architectural enthronements, inscribed prophetic scrolls, elaborate gold ornamentation, and successive representations of the Incarnation, Nativity, Passion, Crucifixion, and Resurrection. 

The resulting composition constitutes an elaborate visual theology of foreknowledge, in which the successive ages of mankind appear as witnesses to an anticipated Redeemer whose advent had been signified through patriarchal promises, prophetic visions, celestial portents, sacrificial prefigurations, and oracular pronouncements.[1]

Particularly significant is the manuscript's commencement with Noah's Ark, an image possessing considerable genealogical, cosmographical, and covenantal implications. The Ark represents the divinely ordained preservation of human ancestry through the destruction of the antediluvian world, inaugurating the subsequent dispersion of nations and the succession of patriarchal generations through which the biblical promises would unfold. 

Genesis 9–11 identifies Shem among the surviving sons of Noah and establishes the succession through Arphaxad, Salah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah, and Abram. 

This genealogical structure supplies an indispensable comparative foundation for examining the relationship between primordial revelation, postdiluvian religious memory, the emergence of national worship, and the eventual particularization of the Abrahamic covenant.

 The additional traditions preserved in Jubilees 7–12 extend this examination through accounts of territorial allotment, ancestral inheritance, calendrical reckoning, the corruption of religious observance, and Abraham's rejection of idolatry. The Apocalypse of Abraham, particularly chapters 1–8, contributes an exceptional narrative of the patriarch's confrontation with manufactured divinities and the spiritual insufficiency of his father's cultic practices. These writings illuminate the religious environment presupposed by Joshua 24:2, where Abraham's ancestors are remembered as worshippers of other gods beyond the Euphrates. 

Collectively, they establish a comparative genealogy of sacred knowledge through which the manuscript's opening Noachic image acquires wider significance, although these additional patriarchal narratives are not themselves represented as independent episodes within the surviving illuminations.[2]

An important textual problem arises within the Arphaxadite succession. The genealogical chronology preserved in the Masoretic text of Genesis 11 differs from that transmitted through the Septuagint, whose Greek succession includes an additional Cainan between Arphaxad and Salah, a figure also appearing in Luke 3:36 in the received Greek New Testament tradition. 

The implications extend beyond numerical chronology into the histories of sacred translation, genealogical authority, textual transmission, and the interpretation of patriarchal antiquity. The Hebrew Tôlĕdôt, the Greek genealogia and genesis, and the Latin generatio provide distinct linguistic avenues for examining descent, origination, and historical continuity. In the context of the manuscript's Christian theology, the postdiluvian succession culminates neither in genealogical curiosity nor in merely antiquarian reconstruction, but in an intelligible progression toward the Abrahamic promise that all families of the earth would receive blessing through his seed, subsequently elaborated through the Mosaic writings, Israelite prophecy, and the New Testament genealogies.[3]

This patriarchal foundation opens an additional and particularly remarkable avenue through the figure of Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High. Genesis 14:18–20 situates his priesthood outside the subsequent Levitical establishment, while Psalm 110:4 and Hebrews 5–7 develop his theological relationship to the enduring priesthood of Christ. 

The Genesis Apocryphon, the Melchizedek traditions associated with 11Q13 from Qumran, and later exegetical materials provide further witnesses to the extraordinary interpretive history of this priestly figure.

 Melchizedek becomes especially pertinent to the manuscript's theological architecture because his biblical appearance demonstrates that legitimate knowledge of the Most High is represented within Scripture beyond the later national priestly institutions of Israel. The precise historical relationship between Melchizedek, Shem, and subsequent Jewish identifications of the two requires separate source-critical examination, yet the existence of that exegetical tradition presents a productive avenue for investigating the preservation of primordial priestly authority.[4]
The appearance of non-Israelite prophetic testimony provides a second indispensable comparison. 

Balaam, son of Beor, whose pronouncements occupy Numbers 22–24, represents an extraordinary biblical instance of an oracle delivered through a foreign seer. His declaration concerning the star proceeding from Jacob and the sceptre arising from Israel in Numbers 24:17 furnished later interpreters with a powerful Messianic text. The relationship between this star oracle, the celestial sign observed by the Magi in Matthew 2, and the wider ancient understanding of astral portents deserves particular attention. The Balaam inscription discovered at Deir Alla, preserving an independent ancient tradition concerning Balaam son of Beor, further establishes the importance of the prophet's reception outside the biblical textual tradition. This constellation of sources offers a historically substantial comparative foundation for exploring the medieval Christian conviction that certain testimonies to divine purposes might appear among peoples beyond Israel. The manuscript's Sibylline witnesses participate in a related Christian theological conception, though their literary histories, claimed antiquity, and textual origins must be distinguished from those of the biblical Balaam traditions.[5]
The twelve Sibyls themselves constitute the manuscript's most conspicuous intellectual and iconographic achievement. Their arrangement reflects the accumulated inheritance of classical antiquity, late antique Christian apologetics, medieval prophetic compilation, and Renaissance manuscript illumination. Varro's enumeration of ten Sibyls, preserved by Lactantius in the Divine Institutes, supplied an influential classificatory precedent, while later traditions expanded the familiar catalogue to twelve, frequently assigning them distinct geographical identities, attributes, and Christological predictions. The Persian, Libyan, Delphic, Cimmerian, Erythraean, Samian, Cumaean, Hellespontine, Phrygian, Tiburtine, and other Sibylline personalities became participants in a remarkable history of religious appropriation and prophetic interpretation. 

Through Christian manuscript culture their supposed announcements were associated with the Virgin Birth, the advent of the Redeemer, the Passion, the Resurrection, and the final judgment. These associations represent a prolonged history of textual transmission and theological attribution. The surviving Sibylline Oracles comprise materials of differing Jewish and Christian provenance, and individual medieval Sibylline sayings cannot invariably be traced to a single ancient exemplar.[6]

Of exceptional importance is the relationship between the Sibylline tradition and the theological testimony of Lactantius, Augustine, and earlier Christian writers who incorporated ancient non-biblical oracles into arguments concerning the antiquity and universality of divine truth. 

Augustine's discussion of the Erythraean Sibyl in De Civitate Dei XVIII. 23 preserves the celebrated Christological acrostic associated with judgment, resurrection, and the return of the divine King. This tradition supplied medieval theologians and artists with a powerful precedent for representing a pagan prophetess as an anticipatory witness to Christian revelation. 

The Oratio ad Sanctorum Coetum, transmitted in association with Constantine, and the broader Christian reception of Virgil's Fourth Eclogue likewise demonstrate the intellectual possibilities opened by interpreting pre-Christian poetry through a Messianic framework. The manuscript's twelve enthroned women must therefore be understood within a long history of authoritative quotation, textual adaptation, geographical classification, prophetic attribution, and artistic personification.[7]

The pictorial apparatus warrants equally detailed consideration. Each Sibylline figure inhabits an architecturally articulated environment incorporating columns, niches, miniature sculptures, pavement geometries, ornamental capitals, elevated thrones, and inscribed scrolls. These architectural settings establish a visual relationship between prophetic knowledge and the authority of its speaker. The enthroned body becomes the center of an ordered symbolic environment, while the scroll externalizes revelation as a legible and transmissible utterance. 

The relationships between bodily gesture, sacred object, costume, enthronement, and written prophecy invite comparison with medieval personifications of Wisdom, Ecclesia, Philosophy, and the prophetic books of the Old Testament. 

The correspondence between the Sibyls' pronouncements and the adjacent biblical scenes is particularly intricate: the manuscript repeatedly transfers the reader's attention from the anticipated event to its illustrated fulfillment, creating a sequential method of biblical exegesis through visual association.

The manuscript's treatment of the Virgin Birth and Incarnation offers further connections with Isaiah 7:14, Isaiah 9:6–7, Micah 5:2, Luke 1–2, and Matthew 1–2. The Annunciation, Nativity, and associated Marian episodes provide a framework for investigating the interpretation of prophetic virginity, the descent of divine Wisdom, angelic communication, the miraculous conception, and the manifestation of the promised child. Proverbs 8–9 contributes an additional theological and philological foundation through the personification of Wisdom, while Sirach 24 and Wisdom of Solomon 7–9 preserve influential Second Temple expressions of divine Wisdom's cosmic operation, purity, radiance, and relationship to creation. The Hebrew ḥokmāh, Greek sophia, Latin sapientia, and Syriac ḥekmtā furnish valuable linguistic correspondences for tracing the reception of Wisdom literature through Jewish and Christian traditions. These sources illuminate the theological vocabulary through which the Incarnation was subsequently interpreted, without requiring the identification of every sapiential image with an explicit prediction of the Virgin Birth.[8]

The Passion sequence, including the humiliation, suffering, and Crucifixion of Christ, brings the manuscript into correspondence with Psalm 22, Isaiah 50:6, Isaiah 52:13–53:12, Zechariah 12:10, Zechariah 13:7, and the New Testament Passion narratives. The suffering servant of Isaiah, the pierced figure of Zechariah, and the righteous sufferer of the Psalter became central elements of Christian Messianic interpretation. 

Their juxtaposition with Sibylline declarations presents a complex instance of retrospective theological harmonization, in which the language of suffering, sacrifice, royal humiliation, and eventual vindication was brought into an encompassing narrative of providential foreknowledge. 

The Resurrection illuminations subsequently draw the sequence toward Psalm 16:10, Isaiah 25:8, Hosea 13:14, and the apostolic exposition of resurrection in Acts 2 and 1 Corinthians 15. The iconographic progression from prophetic announcement to suffering and victory supplies a complete Christological movement whose visual economy merits investigation alongside medieval typological manuscripts, Books of Hours, and illustrated cycles of the Speculum Humanae Salvationis.[9]

The manuscript's importance also extends into historical conceptions of cosmology and celestial signification. The Ark, the prophetic star, the Magi, the heavenly annunciation, and the Resurrection collectively furnish a rich field for examining how sacred history was situated within the perceived relationship between the terrestrial and celestial orders. Ancient Jewish and Christian traditions frequently interpreted astronomical events, angelic appearances, extraordinary lights, and visionary manifestations as significant within providential history.

 The Book of the Watchers in 1 Enoch 6–36, the Astronomical Book in 1 Enoch 72–82, the heavenly journeys of 2 Enoch, and the apocalyptic cosmographies of 2 Baruch and 3 Baruch provide significant comparative materials for investigating celestial hierarchy, visionary ascent, cosmic boundaries, and the symbolic relationship between heavenly realities and earthly events. These works represent distinct literary environments and are not demonstrable textual sources for the manuscript merely by virtue of shared cosmological themes. Nevertheless, they enlarge the historical horizon within which medieval readers understood prophetic visions and celestial testimony.[10]

Further examination of the manuscript's prophetesses invites consideration of the phenomenology of inspired speech, the transmission of prophetic authority, and the relationship between inward revelation and material inscription. The Latin vocabulary of vaticinium, oraculum, revelatio, visio, prophetia, praescientia, and testimonium provides a precise terminological foundation for differentiating prediction, inspired declaration, visionary perception, foreknowledge, and evidentiary witness. 

The Hebrew terms nābîʾ, ḥōzeh, and rōʾeh, together with their Greek and Latin equivalents, permit an extensive comparative inquiry into the identities and activities of ancient seers. 

The manuscript's iconography offers an especially compelling artistic instance of the conversion of spoken or attributed revelation into a permanent written testimony. 

Its scrolls and captions function as material repositories of prophetic statements, while the accompanying images interpret their theological meaning for the reader. 

Such features are indispensable to understanding the historical relationship between revelation, visual exegesis, and manuscript culture.

The exceptional distinction of Sibyllae et Prophetae de Christo Salvatore Vaticinantes ultimately resides in the remarkable concentration of its surviving evidence: primordial covenantal imagery, classical Sibylline personalities, Israelite prophetic testimony, evangelical narration, elaborate architectural iconography, Latin oracular inscriptions, and an ordered visual account of Christian salvation history. 

Its study offers a compelling opportunity to investigate the successive stages through which biblical genealogy, ancient oracular literature, patristic apologetics, medieval prophecy, Renaissance artistic practice, and illuminated manuscript production came into sustained contact. The carefully differentiated use of the Masoretic tradition, Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac biblical witnesses, Qumran literature, Pseudepigrapha, patristic compilations, and early modern antiquarian studies permits the reconstruction of an unusually extensive historical apparatus surrounding this manuscript. 

Through that apparatus, the illuminated Sibyls emerge as witnesses to a major development in Christian intellectual history: the effort to assemble the remembered voices of the ancient world into a universal testimony concerning the promised Messiah.

📜 Scholarly Footnotes & Historical Source Apparatus📜

1. Manuscript identification and prophetic composition.Sibyllae et Prophetae de Christo Salvatore Vaticinantes, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Munich, Cod. icon. 414. Compare the illuminated sequence preserved in the uploaded 51-page digital compilation, particularly pp. 8–32. For the classical and Christian literary foundations of the Sibylline tradition, consult Lactantius, Divinae Institutiones I.6; Augustine, De Civitate Dei XVIII.23; and the surviving Sibylline Oracles. The manuscript's approximate date and workshop attribution should be cited through its institutional catalogue rather than treated as information established solely by the modern presentation title page.

2. The Noachic covenant and Abraham's ancestral religion. Genesis 6–12; Joshua 24:2–3; Jubilees 6–12; Apocalypse of Abraham 1–8; Josephus, Antiquitates Judaicae I.4–7. For modern scholarly translations consult James H. Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, 2 vols. (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1983–1985), especially volume 1 for the Apocalypse of Abraham and volume 2 for Jubilees. See also R. H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees or the Little Genesis (London: Adam and Charles Black, 1902).

3. The Arphaxadite genealogies and ancient textual traditions. Genesis 10:21–32; 11:10–32; 1 Chronicles 1:17–27; Luke 3:34–38; Jubilees 8–12. Consult the Hebrew Masoretic text, the Greek Septuagint, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Latin Vulgate for the relevant genealogical and chronological differences. For the Greek text, see Alfred Rahlfs and Robert Hanhart, eds., Septuaginta, revised edition (Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 2006). Attention should be given to the additional Cainan in the Greek genealogical tradition and its reception in early Christian chronography.

4. Melchizedek, primordial priesthood, and Second Temple interpretation. Genesis 14:18–20; Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 5–7; 11Q13 (11QMelchizedek); Genesis Apocryphon (1Q20). See Joseph A. Fitzmyer, The Genesis Apocryphon of Qumran Cave 1 (1Q20): A Commentary, 3rd ed. (Rome: Pontifical Biblical Institute, 2004). The identification of Melchizedek with Shem belongs to later interpretive tradition and must be distinguished from the explicit wording of Genesis.

5. Balaam and the transmission of foreign prophetic testimony. Numbers 22–24, particularly 24:17; Matthew 2:1–12; the Deir Alla Balaam inscription. For historical investigation of the inscription consult J. Hoftijzer and G. van der Kooij, eds., Aramaic Texts from Deir ʿAlla (Leiden: Brill, 1976). See also Josephus, Antiquitates Judaicae IV.6, for the ancient reception of Balaam's prophetic activity.

6. The Sibylline catalogue and ancient oracular literature. Lactantius, Divinae Institutiones I.6; Sibylline Oracles I–III, VIII; Varro's catalogue as preserved by later authors. For a critical modern treatment consult John J. Collins, “Sibylline Oracles,” in Charlesworth, The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol. 1. See also Milton S. Terry, The Sibylline Oracles Translated from the Greek into English Blank Verse (New York: Eaton & Mains, 1899), for a useful older translation.

7. Patristic reception and Christological acrostics. Augustine, De Civitate Dei XVIII.23; Lactantius, Divinae Institutiones VII; the Oratio ad Sanctorum Coetum attributed to Constantine; Virgil, Eclogue IV. These sources are especially relevant for studying the Christian interpretation of ancient poetry and non-biblical oracular material as anticipations of Christ. Distinguish the antiquity of the named literary authorities from the date and composition of particular Christianized prophecies attributed to them.

8. Wisdom, Incarnation, and multilingual theological vocabulary. Proverbs 3–4; 8–9; Sirach 24; Wisdom of Solomon 7–9; Isaiah 7:14; 9:6–7; Luke 1:26–38; John 1:1–18. Compare the Hebrew, Septuagint, Vulgate, and Syriac Peshitta traditions. For additional Jewish interpretations of divine Wisdom, consult Philo of Alexandria, particularly De Opificio Mundi and De Confusione Linguarum. These sources furnish a substantial intellectual setting for the history of sapiential and incarnational interpretation.

9. Passion typology and medieval pictorial exegesis. Psalm 22; Isaiah 50:6; 52:13–53:12; Zechariah 12:10; 13:7; Psalm 16:10; Hosea 13:14; Luke 24; Acts 2; 1 Corinthians 15. For illustrated medieval typology consult the Biblia Pauperum and the Speculum Humanae Salvationis. See Adrian Wilson and Joyce Lancaster Wilson, A Medieval Mirror: Speculum Humanae Salvationis, 1324–1500 (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1984).

10. Ancient celestial and apocalyptic cosmography. 1 Enoch 6–36 and 72–82; 2 Enoch; 2 Baruch; 3 Baruch; Daniel 7–12; Ezekiel 1 and 10; Revelation 4–5 and 21–22. See Charlesworth, The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vols. 1–2, for translations and introductory material. For the ancient religious and literary development of Jewish apocalyptic thought, consult John J. Collins, The Apocalyptic Imagination: An Introduction to Jewish Apocalyptic Literature (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 2016, 3rd ed.).

Editorial and bibliographical note. 

This abstract combines direct observations from the surviving illuminated manuscript with historical, biblical, pseudepigraphal, and patristic comparative research.

text:
EXPLAINER: Rydberg-atom quantum receivers offer a *fundamentally* different way to detect RF signals. In this post I will explain what exactly Rydberg-atom quantum receivers are, why the Navy is interested in them & ongoing developments in the quantum domain (Global & #Atmanirbhar). 

Rydberg atoms are ordinary alkali atoms (usually cesium or rubidium) excited by lasers to very high energy states. Simply put, in these states the outer electron is far from the nucleus, so the atom becomes extremely sensitive to electric fields.

A typical Rydberg receiver works like this:
* A small glass vapor cell holds the atoms.
* Two lasers create an electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) window.
* An incoming RF or microwave signal (radar, radio, etc.) shifts or splits this window.
* The change is read out optically (by measuring how much laser light passes through the cell).

Key advantages over conventional electronic receivers:-
* Extremely high sensitivity: approaching quantum limits (theoretically tens of dB better SNR in ideal cases).
* Huge frequency coverage: one sensor can span from near-DC to THz by tuning the lasers and atomic states, instead of needing many different antennas.
* Compact & wavelength-independent: the sensing element is a centimeter-scale glass cell connected by fiber optics. Size doesn’t grow with wavelength (a big deal for HF & lower frequencies).
* All-optical readout, self-calibrating & relatively low size/weight/power.
These properties make them attractive for electronic support measures (ESM), signals intelligence (SIGINT), and electronic warfare…detecting, identifying & geolocating enemy radars & communications across a wide spectrum with fewer, smaller sensors.

Global Developments:
U.S. military interest (Army, Navy, DARPA, etc.) in Rydberg sensors has been strong for years. DARPA has run programs such as Quantum Apertures & SAVaNT specifically aimed at portable, high-performance Rydberg RF receivers. Naval research labs have also funded related work (e.g., VHF-band sensing experiments). The goal is better spectrum awareness on ships & other platforms…detecting weak or frequency-agile signals with compact hardware.

AtmanirbharBharat:
India is actively pursuing this. DRDO’s Research Centre Imarat has awarded contracts to @QuBeatsTech for a Rydberg-based Quantum RF Sensor (aimed at electronic support measures / spectrum awareness) alongside a quantum gyroscope. QuBeats is also developing Rydberg RF receivers as part of its quantum sensing portfolio & has an iDEX ADITI contract for a Quantum Positioning System for the Navy.

This is still early days, but the physics is mature and the indigenous effort is underway. I’m happy that indigenous R&D is at par with global state-of-the-art. 

Worth watching closely for ESM, SIGINT & EW applications.

PS: Some may remember #VCNS VAdm Ajay Kochhar stating in the run up to #Swavlamban2026 that quantum technology is a domain the @indiannavy is cognizant of as it works toward multi-domain capabilities. That *was not* just an impressive statement. (Not all details are available in the public domain, so I won’t speak of them). At Swavlamban, people see stalls…#NIIO sees possibilities!

PPS: The “fun test” mentioned is simply a controlled side-by-side comparison: put the quantum receiver & a conventional receiver in the same anechoic chamber, illuminate them with the same signals, and, measure sensitivity, bandwidth, dynamic range, etc. Side-by-side testing against conventional receivers is the logical next step to quantify real-world gains in sensitivity &  bandwidth. Sure sounds like fun😆😉

text:
H.L. Mencken saw this coming almost a century ago.

A diploma can teach you a lot of things. It cannot install common sense. And some of the most credentialed people in America are proving that every semester.

Let's be fair first. A Ph.D. in chemistry or engineering means something. Those fields answer to reality. The bridge holds or it doesn't. The medicine works or it doesn't.

The trouble lives in the departments that answer to nothing but each other.

That's where young people are being taught there are more than two genders, with a whole dictionary of grievances stacked on top.

White privilege. Thin privilege. Systemic ableism. Body fascism. Cisheteropatriarchy. Intersectionality. Epistemic injustice. Settler colonialism. Collective liberation.

Even "adult supremacy," the idea that grownups having authority over kids is a form of oppression.

These aren't punchlines from a late night sketch. They show up in real courses, real syllabi, and real academic books.

The University of Maryland offered "Intro to Fat Studies: Fatness, Blackness and Their Intersections." At the University of New Mexico, the Ph.D. student teaching a fat studies course wrote that she wouldn't grade class participation because doing so is "ableist."

Think about that. Years of graduate school, and the result is someone who believes asking students to speak up in class is discrimination.

Meanwhile, the sticker price at some elite schools now tops $100,000 a year. Families pay it. Taxpayers backstop it through federal loans and grants.

And the people turning out this material get to put "Dr." in front of their names.

Mencken's point was simple. The credential doesn't change what's underneath. If someone can't tell reality from fantasy going in, a diploma won't fix it coming out.

You can hand them the degree. You can frame it and hang it on the wall. You can add three letters after their name.

You can't change stupid.

Who has more common sense, the professors at Harvard or the people who fix your truck, wire your house, and run the farm down the road?

text:
🔬 UPCOMING SCIENCE: NASA'S NEW LUNAR EXPERIMENTS AND A MAJOR MERCURY MILESTONE

Two developments worth watching: NASA has selected three new investigations for the Moon, and an international spacecraft is approaching a major orbital milestone at Mercury.

These projects involve underground lunar structures, water ice, lunar seismic activity and the interior and magnetic environment of Mercury.

🌕 1. NASA SELECTS THREE NEW LUNAR SCIENCE INVESTIGATIONS

On September 30, 2026, NASA announced three new payload investigations selected through its PRISM program. They are intended to support lunar exploration and future operations at NASA's planned Moon Base.

The instruments are expected to travel to the Moon through NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services program.

LEMS-SP — Lunar Environment Monitoring Station, South Pole

This investigation is designed to monitor the lunar environment over time.

Its work includes:
• Detecting seismic events with a short-period seismometer.
• Monitoring micrometeoroid impacts.
• Measuring the abundance of volatile materials around the lunar surface.
The goal is to better understand environmental hazards that could affect equipment and future astronauts.
Principal investigator: Dr. Mehdi Benna, University of Maryland, Baltimore County.
GIMLI — Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar Pit Investigation

This is one of the more unusual projects.

NASA plans to investigate the Marius Hills Pit, a large opening on the Moon that may lead into an underground lava tube.

The instrument package will scan beneath the surface to determine whether a substantial underground cavern exists.

Why it matters:
• Underground lava tubes could offer protection from radiation.
• They could provide more stable temperatures than the exposed lunar surface.
• They may offer natural protection from micrometeoroid impacts.

The existence and dimensions of a usable underground shelter still need to be confirmed.

Principal investigator: Dr. Nathaniel Putzig, Planetary Science Institute.

The current GIMLI development schedule points toward a possible launch and landing around 2031. It does not yet have a confirmed launch provider or exact launch date.
DISCO — Depth Imager with Spectral and Color Optics
This investigation is designed to make direct measurements of water ice hidden in extremely cold lunar regions known as micro-cold traps.
It will also study:
• Where lunar ice exists.
• How much ice is present.
• How rocket exhaust disturbs lunar soil.
• How the surface behaves for future rover movement and operations.

Principal investigator: Dr. Ariel Deutsch, NASA Ames Research Center.

Direct measurements could help establish how much usable water may actually exist on the Moon.

🚀 2. BEPICOLOMBO: MERCURY ORBIT INSERTION ON NOVEMBER 21

Another important upcoming event is scheduled for November 21, 2026.

The joint European Space Agency and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency BepiColombo mission is approaching Mercury after approximately eight years of travel.

The mission consists of two orbiters traveling together:
• ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO).
• JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, called Mio.
They are designed to study Mercury from different orbital positions.
Their investigations include:
• Mercury's internal structure and composition.
• Its magnetic field.
• Its surface and polar deposits.
• Its thin exosphere.
• Its interaction with the solar environment.
The upcoming timeline:

November 21, 2026 — The spacecraft composite is scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury.

December 9–10, 2026 — The two orbiters are scheduled to separate.

April 2027 — The mission's dedicated science phase is expected to begin.

The November 21 event is an orbital insertion milestone. It is not the start of the full two-orbiter science campaign.

WHY THESE DEVELOPMENTS MATTER

The lunar projects could answer practical questions about underground shelters, water resources and environmental hazards before humans attempt longer stays on the Moon.

BepiColombo will provide a much more detailed study of Mercury, one of the least explored planets in our Solar System.
Both projects are moving beyond orbital photographs toward direct measurements and detailed investigations.

text:
🌍 Morning Global Briefing · Nov 03, 2026

POLITICS
• US midterms are underway today: polls favor Democrats to take the House, with the Senate within reach, a result that would sharply constrain President Trump's agenda.
• The US Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's emergency bid to set aside more than 20,000 California mail-in ballots, so all cast ballots stay in the count.
• Russian strikes resumed after a local ceasefire in southern Ukraine expired, with at least 26 killed at a school where aid was being handed out; US envoy Witkoff says Ukraine, US and Russia officials will meet in Abu Dhabi next week for preliminary talks.
• Iran calls its indirect talks with Washington "very intensive," but the IMO still warns that the Strait of Hormuz is unsafe because of possible mines.
• Belgian PM Bart De Wever tendered his resignation after budget talks failed; King Philippe has not yet decided whether to accept it.

ECONOMY
• Wall Street closed mixed: the Dow rose 0.41% while the S&P 500 fell 0.51% and the Nasdaq fell 1.07%, as a chip selloff pushed the Nasdaq 100 into a technical correction.
• Brent fell 7.63% to $104.77 on US-Iran peace hopes, its biggest drop since April, then edged back up in Asian trade after a report of a US strike on Iran's Qeshm Island.
• Bitcoin slipped 1.5% to about $76,650 and gold rose 1.9% to about $3,947, while the US 10-year yield eased to around 4.90%.
• South Korea's Kospi dropped more than 3.5% on tech weakness; the RBA is expected to raise rates to 4.85% today, its fifth hike this year.

TECH
• Marvell agreed to buy optical networking firm Lumentum for $115 billion, and Marvell fell 13% while Lumentum fell 19% as investors questioned the price of the AI buildout.
• Oracle plans to raise about $20 billion through stock and bonds to fund AI infrastructure; Apple fell about 2% after hours on a disappointing margin outlook.
• DeepSeek open-sourced Super-Agent, a coding agent that watches team chats and offers fixes unprompted.

SPORTS
• Kimi Antonelli finished third in Mexico City to become, at 20, the youngest F1 World Champion ever and the first Italian champion since Ascari in 1953; Verstappen won the race.
• Luka Dončić posted 45 points, 15 rebounds, 6 assists and 5 steals in the Lakers' 131-125 win over Toronto, a stat line never recorded before in NBA history.

HEALTH & SOCIETY
• Two UN reports warn that overshooting 1.5°C of warming would bring irreversible damage to glaciers, sea ice and Earth's frozen regions.
• All 69 victims of last week's high-speed train collision in Urda, Spain, have been identified, and 29 people remain in hospital.

text:
Today on Earth, Russian bombs struck a humanitarian-aid distribution center and a nearby shelter in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, killing 26 people, Ukrainian officials said. About 20 others were missing, and rescuers reported further drone attacks during the response. Separately, cyberattacks sent false nuclear, chemical and other emergency warnings through government alert apps in both Ukraine and Russia; authorities did not establish whether the breaches were connected.

Iranian negotiators left Doha after three days of indirect talks with Qatari mediators produced revised proposals but no breakthrough toward ending the U.S.-Iran war. Iran said contacts were continuing. Oil prices fell about 7% on hopes that diplomacy could eventually reopen the Strait of Hormuz and ease supply disruptions.

On the eve of the U.S. midterm elections, more than 54 million Americans had voted early. The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s emergency request to require California to set aside about 20,000 mail ballots belonging to people federal officials alleged might be noncitizens. California said the list contained errors and risked disenfranchising eligible voters; the justices gave no explanation and recorded no public dissents.

Election Day is tomorrow. Naturally, the lawyers arrived first.

Federal investigators said parts of the Learjet 60 that crashed Sunday in Palm Beach County, Florida, may have broken away before impact. All nine people aboard were killed. The National Transportation Safety Board had not determined what caused the jet’s rapid descent.

A cyberattack manipulated refrigeration systems at supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland and Estonia, raising temperatures and forcing stores to discard food. No group claimed responsibility, and investigators had not established whether the incidents were connected to a similar attack in France last month.

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever offered his resignation after coalition talks over €10 billion in spending cuts and tax increases collapsed. King Philippe did not immediately accept it and began consultations with coalition leaders.

Britain announced that many migrants will have to wait 10 years instead of five for permanent residency. High earners and qualifying public-service workers can settle sooner, while people who entered illegally by small boat could wait as long as 30 years.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration tentatively approved an inexpensive generic version of lenacapavir, a twice-yearly HIV-prevention injection. The drug is expected to cost about $40 per person annually and could expand access in 120 low- and middle-income countries, though local approvals and funding are still required.

Uganda began withdrawing troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of fighting al-Shabab. The phased drawdown is scheduled to remove all Ugandan forces by the end of 2027.

Japan launched a national disaster-management agency to coordinate preparedness, emergency response and reconstruction. The agency will focus on threats including major earthquakes, tsunamis and a possible Mount Fuji eruption.

On this day in 1936, the BBC launched the world’s first regular high-definition television service from Alexandra Palace in London.

That was one day on Earth.

See you tomorrow. Same planet. Europe’s refrigerators were hacked, but America’s election lawyers remain fully operational. 🌎

text:
Editor's Pick | On 3 November 1970, Salvador Allende became the first socialist president of Chile. Born in 1908, in Valparaíso, into an upper-middle-class family, Allende helped found the Socialist Party in 1933. Allende, seen here giving a speech, in 1962, at a solidarity rally for the Cuban Revolution, had a long political career.

Though he had been a senator four times, Allende had lost three presidential bids before 1970, when he ran as the candidate for Popular Unity, a coalition of socialists, communists, radicals and dissident Christian democrats. After his win, Allende set out to restructure Chilean society along socialist lines while retaining democratic institutions. His government nationalised the copper industry, much of which was controlled by companies from the United States; established peasant cooperatives, which took over large agricultural estates; authorised large wage increases; and froze prices.

In response, the United States blocked foreign loans and the Central Intelligence Agency spent over $8 million funding activities to disrupt Allende’s presidency, including strikes and opposition media. By 1972, Chile was experiencing stagnant production, rising inflation, food shortages and widespread unrest.

Allende’s coalition still won nearly half of the vote in the election held in March 1973. His second term was short-lived, as a coup d’état led by Augusto Pinochet overthrew the government in September that year. Allende refused an offer of safe passage out of the country, and on 11 September 1937, he died—apparently by suicide—after the air force bombed the presidential palace.

Energy sector −3.96%; tech −2.95%

This was the first session of November. The Dow rose while the tech-heavy indexes fell.

Biggest stories
Marvell ($MRVL) agreed to buy Lumentum ($LITE), and AI-hardware stocks sold off.All-stock deal: 4.5 $MRVL shares per $LITE share, implied enterprise value about $115bn.
$LITE −18.59%, $MRVL −12.72%, Ciena ($CIEN) −11.34%.
Marvell says the deal will save more than $1bn a year (the company’s own claim).
$STX, $WDC, $AMD, $DELL and $MU each fell 5.8–7.9%.

Oracle ($ORCL) plans to raise $20bn to pay for its AI buildout. It filed to sell $10bn of new shares and $10bn of bonds.
The stock fell 8.76%, and the news revived worries about how AI spending gets funded.

Oil fell more than 7% on hopes for Iran peace talks.Reports said Iran’s supreme leader allowed the government to hold peace talks. Iran also offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions.
WTI’s 7.36% drop was its biggest one-day fall since Jul 27.
Energy was the worst sector (−3.96%): Occidental ($OXY) −5.12%, Exxon ($XOM) −4.02%. Airlines and grocers rose.

Factory data was strong, but construction spending fell.ISM manufacturing rose to 55.5 from 54.5 (forecast 54.5–54.6). Production was 59.0, the highest since Nov 2021.
Prices paid eased to 75.2 from 77.9.
September construction spending fell 1.9% (forecast +0.4%).

$PLTR: revenue $2.313bn (+96%) vs $2.17bn expected; full-year guidance raised to $8.53bn. It closed −3.13% and was +1.32% after hours.

text:
THE MOST ADVANCED ORGANIZATION IN AMERICA WAS REACHED THROUGH THE BUSINESS SOFTWARE — AND THE ARGUMENT NOW IS OVER WHAT COUNTS AS "THE FULL EXTENT"

SCOPE FIRST. This was an authorized security-testing engagement under Anthropic's cybersecurity testing/bug bounty program, reported by the Washington Post on Oct 26 — a week ago. BNN missed it on every sweep since; we are catching up, and saying so plainly. Not a crime, not an intrusion in the ordinary sense: a test, a report, and now a fight about the report.

THE TWO ACCOUNTS. Cathedral — a months-old cybersecurity start-up founded by four former Department of Government Efficiency staffers (Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, Marko Elez, Jack Stein), valued at $1.4 billion, $160 million raised from Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital — told Anthropic its AI agents had found ways into the company's internal systems by exploiting vulnerabilities in third-party business software. Cathedral's account, per the Post: the agents took less than 12 hours to find paths to sensitive information — meeting transcripts, salaries and job offers, Slack messages. Anthropic's account, per the same reporting: the researchers had previously spent several days unsuccessfully trying to breach its software directly. Both halves ride together. The advanced part of the organization was not the part that broke.

WHAT ANTHROPIC CONFIRMS: the researchers gained access to a "limited set" of its sales, human resources and IT systems — customer and partner business contact information and some basic user account records. And what it rules out, carried in full every time: the researchers did not access Claude users' conversations, source code, or AI model weights.

WHERE IT BROKE DOWN IS THE DISCLOSURE. Both sides agree the researchers reported. Anthropic says Cathedral violated the program's rules by failing to disclose the full extent of its activity. Cathedral's draft report — reviewed by the Post, never published — says this: "The fact that weaknesses in ordinary enterprise software can compromise the infrastructure of even the most advanced organizations should be a wake-up call for every company in America."

THE VENDOR'S OWN DEFENCE, verbatim to the Post: "Our monitoring flagged some of Cathedral's activity before they reported it to us." Anthropic says it shut off the start-up's access the same day, pulled the vulnerable tools out of service until the vendors confirmed the flaws were addressed, and briefed federal officials.

THE REGISTER WE CARE ABOUT. (1) The perimeter was never the model. Days against Anthropic's own software went nowhere; the way in was ordinary third-party business software — the class every operator already trusts by default. (2) The disclosure fight is now about granularity, not existence: not whether there was a report, but what it should have said was reached. (3) An unnamed senior Trump administration official said the episode raised national security concerns — about whether similar weaknesses could be abused by others. That is a fear about a hypothetical, not a finding. (4) Reported background, no causal link drawn: Kliger was previously the Pentagon's chief data officer and was reportedly involved in the Pentagon's fallout with Anthropic.

NO TECHNICAL DETAIL RUNS HERE BY DESIGN. The third-party software is unnamed at every source, and we are keeping it unnamed. Cathedral's claims come from a draft report we have not read; Anthropic's statements are the company's own. Each side's wording is attributed and left standing.

text:
The Novus Ordo vs the SSPX: Where do you come down?

A couple of years ago, I went to Tokyo to give a talk to the traditional Catholic community in Japan’s de facto capitol. While there, I discovered that there is just one Traditional Latin Mass in all of Japan. It is offered by Father Thomas Onoda of the Society of St. Pius X.

Father Onoda is quite literally the sole missionary priest in the largest city in the world. No FSSP, no ICK, no diocesan Latin Masses in Tokyo. And I wonder if those who rail against the SSPX are aware that this is how it is in many countries. The SSPX is the only game in town.

So, here’s my question for the critics: Would it be better if there were no Latin Mass in Tokyo at all? Would you prefer to see Japanese traditional Catholics attending the very progressive Novus Ordo Masses in Japan with no TLM option?

If the answer is in the affirmative, then Cardinal Arthur Roche is right -- we all need to get over ourselves! The fight for the TLM is merely a matter of personal preference. It has nothing to do with principle, orthodoxy, or revolution/counterrevolution. What we all need to do is comply with the Novus Ordo regime no matter what . . . so says Cardinal Roche.

But what say you?

In the wake of Traditionis Custodes and the subsequent barring of the Summorum Pontificum Pilgrimage from St. Peter’s in Rome last weekend, this is a matter of growing urgency. We need to get this right. The noose is tightening, and we are obviously running out of time.

In my new Underground, I do a deep dive into this and into the larger, contextual question of Preference v Counterrevolution. Check it out (link in comments) and let me know your thoughts.

[1/2]

Leon felt like he hadn’t slept in centuries, and he desperately needed coffee. Strong and bitter, something that would wake him up for real. While working as a private detective, he had another missing person case to solve, and he had already spent so much time and energy on it, with no help.

He entered the first coffee shop he came across, which appeared to be one of those places he didn’t quite hate but didn’t fully understand either: a hipster café. Leon didn’t fancy their music or overly polished style. However, this one seemed to be different: it was playing old rock music, had multiple posters of bands on the walls, and featured a rather vintage look, with furniture in red and black.

Leon took off his gloves and approached the barista, who had his back turned to him. The guy was whistling along to the melody of Highway to Hell, seeming to be in his own little world so early in the morning. Leon was also the only customer in the place at this hour.

The barista felt Leon’s gaze on him and turned around. He appeared to be a young guy with piercing brown eyes and short, dark hair. He was much younger than Leon, yet still taller. His muscular build seemed a little out of place in this stylish yet cozy establishment, and Leon wondered what a guy like him was doing here. Well, apart from working.

Leon also noticed a name badge on the barista’s apron: Chris.

“Oh, wow.” Chris couldn’t hide his surprise. “That’s the first time I’ve seen an early bird like you here, sir. You came for some coffee or some company?”

Leon raised an eyebrow. Was it… flirting? From a guy half his age?

This kid must be joking.

“Coffee would work,” Leon answered almost carelessly, though his interest had grown. The guy was saying some pretty bold things, but the way he shifted his weight from one foot to the other and kept adjusting his short hair, which hardly needed any attention, was a curious contrast. “Black. No sugar.”

The barista whistled.

“Figures. No sweetness in this life?”

Leon shrugged.

“Not in the morning, for sure.” Leon paid for his coffee, and Chris got to work, still glancing at Kennedy as he worked his coffee magic.

“I prefer sweets during nighttime, too.”

The phrase seemed innocent enough, but the way the barista looked at Leon… made the older man shift uncomfortably.

“I’ve never seen you around before. A new neighbor?” Chris asked.

“Something like that. Just looking for someone.”

Leon could have shown Chris a photo of the missing man and asked if he knew anything, but he didn’t want to risk leaking the details of his investigation to a younger guy he had just met.

“Maybe I can help?” Chris narrowed his eyes. “I know everyone around here.”

For the first time in weeks, Leon felt something tug at the corners of his mouth. Something almost like a smile, but not quite.

“Are you always that curious?”

“Only with handsome customers.”

Leon’s breath hitched for a moment.

Okay, that was definitely flirting.

He cleared his throat.

“I’m not interested in youngsters.”

Chris poured the coffee and handed him the cup with a sly smile.

“And I don’t usually offer information to people who sneak around… but there are exceptions, right?”

Leon looked at the cup, then at Chris.

How did he know Leon was sneaking around? There was something fishy about this guy.

Their fingers brushed as Leon finally took his cup.

ENJOY NOW, SUFFER LATER… OR SUFFER NOW, ENJOY LATER?

Life is full of choices. Every day, we make decisions that may bring temporary happiness or eternal consequences. The world offers pleasure, entertainment, alcohol, worldly desires, and a lifestyle that makes people forget about God. It promises happiness today, but never tells you about the price you may pay tomorrow.

Many people are willing to sacrifice their relationship with God just to enjoy a few moments of worldly pleasure. They choose temporary satisfaction over eternal salvation. They exchange prayer for entertainment, holiness for popularity, and obedience for personal desires.

But remember this: Not everything that feels good is good for your soul. Not everything that makes you happy today will lead you to a joyful eternity.

Following Jesus is not always easy. Sometimes you must say no to temptation when everyone else says yes. Sometimes you must walk away from sinful pleasures, endure persecution, remain faithful when life becomes difficult, and choose holiness even when nobody is watching.

You may suffer now because you refuse to compromise your faith. You may be mocked because you stand for biblical truth. You may be rejected because you choose to obey God. But never forget that temporary suffering for Christ is far better than temporary pleasure that leads you away from Him.

The Bible reminds us:

Romans 8:18 (KJV)
"For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us."

And Jesus said:

Matthew 16:26 (KJV)
"For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?"

Think about that!

What is the value of having everything this world can offer if you lose your soul? What is the benefit of enjoying every sinful pleasure today if you neglect the eternal destiny of your soul?

Church, wake up! Life is short. Eternity is forever. Do not allow temporary pleasures to destroy your eternal future.

Choose Jesus over the world. Choose holiness over compromise. Choose obedience over disobedience. Choose the narrow way, even when it is difficult.

SUFFER NOW, REMAIN FAITHFUL, AND LOOK FORWARD TO THE ETERNAL GLORY THAT GOD HAS PROMISED.

Don't live only for today. Live with eternity in mind!

🔥 THE PLEASURES OF SIN ARE TEMPORARY, BUT ETERNITY HAS NO END.

text:
If you walk into a room of eleven people who have already made up their minds, and you yell, "You are all wrong," what happens?

They don't listen to you. They lock the door, cross their arms, and fight you twice as hard.

Yet I watch you and your sales team do this every single week.

A buyer gets on a call with you. Their brain is already made up. Maybe they use your biggest competitor. Maybe they use a messy spreadsheet they built five years ago. Either way, they feel safe where they are. They just want to get through your thirty-minute call and get back to their real day.

And what does your team do?

They open a forty-slide deck and start shouting about how great your company is. Look at our features! Look at our speed! Look at how much money we will save you!

You are standing at the table screaming, "The boy is innocent!" to eleven people who already have their coats on.

Go back and watch the first twenty minutes of the movie 12 Angry Men.

Twelve men walk into a hot, locked room to decide if a kid is guilty of murder. Eleven of them raise their hands for "guilty" right away. One guy literally has tickets to a baseball game that night and wants to leave in five minutes.

Only one man—Juror #8—raises his hand for "not guilty."

Watch what he does next, because it is a masterclass in how human brains actually change.

When the other eleven men yell at him and ask if he really believes the kid is innocent, Juror #8 doesn't say yes. He doesn't bang his fist on the table. He doesn't pitch a big story.

He looks at them quietly and says, "I don't know."

He says, "This boy's life is worth five minutes of talking. Maybe you are right. Let's just look at the pieces one more time."

Why does he do that?

Because he knows that the human brain is lazy. Thinking hurts. So whenever our brains can take a shortcut and stay on autopilot, they do. As long as those eleven men feel 100% sure of their old story, their brains are completely closed. If you try to push a brand-new answer into a closed head, it bounces right off.

You cannot sell a new truth to someone who is still comfortable with their old story. Before you can give them an answer, you have to give them a splinter of doubt.

Watch how Juror #8 plants that splinter.

The whole murder case rests on a fancy switchblade with a carved handle found at the crime scene. The store owner swore in court that it was the only knife like it in the whole neighbourhood. That knife is the reason all eleven men feel safe voting guilty.

If Juror #8 were a normal B2B CEO, he would give a twenty-minute speech about how store owners sometimes lie. Nobody would believe him.

Instead, he waits until everyone is staring at the murder weapon in the middle of the table. Then he reaches into his own coat pocket, pulls out a second knife, and sticks it into the wood right next to the first one.

It is the exact same knife. He bought it the night before at a pawn shop two blocks from the boy's house for six dollars.

The room goes dead silent.

He didn't win the whole trial with that move. He did something much more important: he broke their autopilot. He forced eleven lazy brains to wake up and ask three quiet words:

"Is it possible?"

Once a buyer asks themselves, "Is it possible that what we are doing right now isn't actually safe?" — you don't have to push anymore. They start pulling.

By the end of the movie, Juror #8 never forces a single man to change his vote. He just keeps asking quiet questions about the things they took for granted (a slow old man walking to a door, a woman who wears glasses to see out a window) until their old story falls apart under its own weight.

Now look at how you talk to buyers today.

When growth slows down, and buyers tell you, "We're fine with how we do things right now,"* you keep trying to make your pitch louder. You add more slides. You brag harder about your AI. You offer a 20% discount to make them move.

You are arguing with a closed room.

Your buyer doesn't care about your solution because they don't yet doubt their own safety. They think the store owner's knife is the only one in town.

Stop pitching "innocent" in the first five minutes. Stop telling buyers everything your product can do.

Instead, look at the comfortable lie your buyer tells themselves every morning to feel safe doing nothing. Then ask yourself one question:

What is the $6 knife I can drop on the table in the first five minutes that breaks their autopilot without me saying a word?

text:
So yeah, just watched #GodzillaMinusZero aka #ゴジラ-0 in its UK Premiere at the BFI IMAX and I’m OVERWHELMED! #TakashiYamazaki definitely went much bigger delivering the most satisfying, epic, yet heartbreaking sequel featuring #Godzilla.

Never a Godzilla film felt and looked so overwhelmingly devastating. Differently from #GodzillaMinusOne, the monsters and their destructive actions are way more prominent in the new instalment. And visually, #Ghidorah and #Godzilla reached their best forms yet. If the previous film was more like a war drama with #Godzilla in it, this one is a Kaiju feast, with an even more impressive VFX work than what we saw in the first.

But the human aspect remains the why this series of Godzilla films works so much more than whatever we’ve seen before. You care about those human individuals and about everything they went through because of these monsters, and even when the monsters are front and center showcasing their full glory, it’s the characters on the ground you are still worrying about. Will they survive? Will their many kinds of sacrifices pay off?

It’s a movie about living with wounds, fear & trauma - not overcoming or healing them, at best adapting your life to accommodate them as your new normal (sounds familiar?), for a nation still plagued by the scars left by the war, while the film uses two monsters as allegories of a nation caught in the middle of the Cold War tensions between the two superpowers U.S. and the USRR.

The stakes are much higher this time around - and the American army much more involved, and some interesting ethical and moral questions are layered throughout the film - some clearly aimed at #Oppenheimer himself, but also at our masterminds of today: the fact that you could meddle with a power beyond your comprehension doesn’t mean you should.

New life lessons of bravery, self donation, empathy,  the worth of standing up for what you believe, but also the thirst for revenge, or the naivety of allowing yourself to engage in a selfish pursuit of a normal, happy life when the world around you is on the edge of complete collapse, really make us root even more for the characters - and suffer for them when things don’t quite go their way.

All of that highlighted by an INCREDIBLE sound design and scores throughout this film, and really helping you to feel immersed in the feels of danger, desolation and powerlessness facing mass destruction.

#GodzillaMinusZero succeeds in finding the delicate balance no Kaiju film could achieve before: being an epic monster film while also working as an epic human drama, without ever making us feel like any of those two sides are overstaying or taking away the spotlight from each other, or that we are getting too little from one at the expense of the other. It’s an incredible cinematic event for the biggest screen possible, while also repeating that deeply connection with the human characters we loved so much on the first one.

Also, I loved that the film even found time to pay homage to all timers such as TITANIC.

And I swear, when you watch this film, the impression you get is that it’s a 200M budgeted blockbuster. How they managed to pull those visuals off with a rumoured 15M budget I have absolute no idea. No movie released this year looks nearly as good or expensive-looking as this one. It’s just INSANE! 

To summarise, #GodzillaMinusZero is a triumph as a sequel which elevates the spectacle while never losing track of the human drama which conquered our hearts in the previous one. It’s a visual delight and an emotional saga, which offers deeper conversations to be unearthed once we manage to see beyond the allegorical creatures and events, that are not only about post-war Japan, but can easily find parallels in our own current world.

One last thing… Akiko!

#GodzillaMinusZero debuts in Japan TOMORROW, NOV 03, and in the U.S. on FRI NOV 06.

text:
Nov 3, 1984: For two agonising days, our lives hung in the balance. The government’s inaction left us suffocating in isolation, our minds consumed by terror as reports of mass killings, the degradation of women, and burning homes closed in. The psychological walls were collapsing. Aware of our hideouts were known to many by then, a grim resolve took over: we gathered at our home to face our fate together. Trapped and desperate, a sudden, fierce rage overtook me. I gripped a sword, ready to charge the butchers outside, only to be broken by the sight of my sobbing parents begging me to stay.
The terror peaked when we were offered to be taken elsewhere, but our visible Sikh identity felt like a target on our backs, rendering us completely trapped. Then came a moment of profound, soul-crushing agony. We, who had never touched a blade to our hair, had to cut it. As the shears met our hair, we clung to one another, weeping violently, feeling as though our very souls and identities were being erased. The despair was so total that my father, broken by the humiliation, tried to take his own life with a pair of scissors. He said, “this is the second Partition for me”. 
When a few Army men finally arrived at 2:45 PM, the relief was tangled with grief. We profusely thanked our Hindu neighbours with heavy heart who had shielded us, left our home unlocked in their hands, and stepped into the ruins of our world.
The one-kilometre walk to the Army truck forced us through an indescribable nightmare. The streets had a few half-burned bodies and damaged properties though the realisation that most had been incinerated alive inside their homes was sickening. The ultimate horror struck when I saw an animal dragging the remains of a devout, recognisable GurSikh—a sight that left me utterly paralysed with grief.
Boarding the truck, the collective trauma was overwhelming. Every familiar face was broken, wailing for lost families. We were finally dropped at the Delhi Cantt Sadar Bazar Gurdwara Sahib, finding cold comfort among 200 odd other shattered families who shared our profound loss. The Gurdwara Sahib was going to be our abode for the next tens of days.

🔑 Extra Note Worthy Information: The Twelve Oracular Thrones & the Prophetic Architecture of Salvation - The opening illustration of Noah's Ark possesses an interpretive significance far beyond its pictorial function. Within a collection otherwise devoted to the pronouncements of twelve ancient prophetesses, the vessel of the Deluge introduces a primordial boundary between the destruction of the first inhabited world and the subsequent dispersion of its surviving generations. 

The Ark thus establishes a genealogical and covenantal foundation from which the manuscript's subsequent testimonies may be examined.

This is especially remarkable when read alongside Genesis 9–11, the genealogical materials in Jubilees, the ancestral traditions preserved by Josephus, and the later literature concerning Abraham's departure from ancestral idolatry. 

The sequence Noah → Shem → Arphaxad → Abraham → Moses → Prophets → Christ provides a substantial additional framework for investigating the manuscript's prophetic theology. 

It is a framework developed through comparative interpretation, rather than a genealogy explicitly reproduced in the illuminations themselves.

The manuscript's twelve Sibyls represent another dimension of the same investigation. Their attributed testimonies came to occupy an extraordinary position in Christian historical theology, particularly through the writings of Lactantius, Augustine, and traditions associated with the Sibylline Oracles. Figures originating in Persian, Libyan, Delphic, Cimmerian, Erythraean, Samian, Cumaean, Hellespontine, Phrygian, Tiburtine, and other oracular traditions entered the Christian imagination as witnesses to the coming Redeemer.

The actual relationship between these figures and the surviving prophetic texts varies considerably. 

Nevertheless, the manuscript offers an exceptional opportunity to investigate the historical transmission of their attributed pronouncements, the successive Christian reinterpretations of ancient oracular literature, and the theological techniques by which apparently distant testimonies were assembled into one visual sequence.

Its illuminated narrative incorporates the Nativity, Marian episodes, Christ's suffering, the Crucifixion, Resurrection, and further events of salvation history. Each representation becomes part of a carefully ordered dialogue between prediction and fulfillment.

Particularly impressive are the architectural thrones upon which the prophetesses sit. Their columns contain carved figures and miniature images; their interiors contain vaulted recesses, patterned floors, and elevated seating. Their garments, ritual implements, books, staffs, vessels, and accompanying inscriptions establish a distinctive iconography for each prophetic personality. Such features invite detailed treatment through historical iconography, manuscript palaeography, Christian symbolism, architectural phenomenology, and the history of visionary literature.
The manuscript also preserves a significant intellectual question: How did Christian scholars and artists understand the possibility that the ancient nations possessed fragments of foreknowledge concerning Israel's Messiah?

That question extends backward into the Hebrew Bible itself, where Balaam, Melchizedek, Job, and certain foreign rulers and sages occupy important positions outside the ordinary prophetic succession of Israel. It also extends into Second Temple literature, Josephus, the writings of early Christian apologists, and Renaissance efforts to catalogue ancient wisdom.

II. The Genesis–Abrahamic–Mosaic Correspondence - 

PROPOSED COMPARATIVE RESEARCH SEQUENCE

01
Noah and the antediluvian inheritance
Genesis 6–9 · Jubilees 5–7 · Manuscript PDF p. 8

02
Shem and the postdiluvian nations
Genesis 9:26–27; 10–11 · Jubilees 8–9

03
Arphaxad and the patriarchal succession
Genesis 10:22; 11:10–26 · Luke 3:34–36

04
Abraham, Ur, and the ancestral idols
Genesis 11:27–12:3 · Joshua 24:2 · Jubilees 12 · Apocalypse of Abraham 1–8

05
Moses and the non-Israelite oracle
Numbers 22–24 · Numbers 24:17 · Deuteronomy 18:15–19

06
Messianic testimony and fulfillment
Isaiah 7, 9, 11, 53 · Micah 5 · Zechariah 9, 12–13 · Gospel accounts

One particularly fruitful direction concerns Genesis 11:10–26 and Luke 3:34–36. These passages preserve the ancestral succession leading toward Abraham, though the Greek genealogical tradition includes an additional Cainan between Arphaxad and Salah that is absent from the Masoretic sequence.

 This textual distinction opens an extensive investigation into the Septuagint, the Samaritan Pentateuch, Jubilees, and early chronographic traditions.
In Jubilees12, Abraham's rejection of ancestral idolatry becomes a developed narrative. 

The Apocalypse of Abraham1–8 supplies another account of the young patriarch confronting the worship of manufactured deities. These materials illuminate Joshua 24:2, which recalls the foreign gods worshipped by Abraham's forefathers beyond the Euphrates.
The manuscript itself does not depict those traditions directly, but its opening Noachic miniature makes them especially relevant to a fuller study of sacred ancestral succession.

Even more closely related to its subject is Numbers 24:17, where Balaam, a foreign diviner, announces the star proceeding from Jacob and the sceptre arising from Israel. Balaam provides an important biblical point of comparison for the medieval understanding of non-Israelite prophetic testimony. The comparison can then be carried into Matthew 2 and the Magi, with careful distinction between the biblical texts and later interpretive associations.
