text:
The AI Productivity Trap: Companies Are Measuring the Wrong Things

When Everyone Can Produce More, What Actually Becomes Valuable?

I have been thinking about a strange contradiction in the AI economy.

Companies are buying AI subscriptions, deploying agents, training employees, and encouraging everyone to use more artificial intelligence.

Some are even measuring how many tokens employees consume.

But there is a question that seems to receive much less attention:

Are these companies actually becoming more valuable?

On October 28, 2026, a report from Gartner revealed something worth examining: only 3% of surveyed organizations said they had achieved their targets for productivity, efficiency, and cost reduction through AI.

At the same time, 85% of surveyed leaders planned to increase AI spending in 2027, while 38% were already over budget.

That is an interesting contradiction.

The technology is spreading rapidly. Corporate spending is accelerating. Expectations remain enormous.

Yet measurable business results are proving much harder to achieve.

I don't think this necessarily means AI is overhyped.

I think it reveals a deeper problem with how businesses understand productivity.

1. Producing More Is Not the Same as Creating More Value

Imagine two employees.

The first employee uses AI to generate 50 reports every day.

The second employee uses AI to identify one recurring operational problem that has been costing the company hundreds of thousands of dollars.

The first employee produces more visible output.

The second employee creates more economic value.

But which employee would look more productive on a dashboard measuring AI usage?

This is where I believe many organizations are making a fundamental mistake.

They are confusing activity with outcomes.

AI can make it dramatically cheaper to produce:

Reports.
Software code.
Marketing content.
Financial analysis.
Customer communications.
Research documents.

But none of these outputs automatically creates revenue, customer loyalty, competitive advantage, or sustainable profits.

A company can generate ten times more content and still acquire no additional customers.

It can write software faster and still release a product nobody wants.

It can automate customer support and still lose customers because the experience becomes worse.

The cost of producing something is not the same as the value of producing it.

This distinction becomes increasingly important as production costs approach zero.

2. The Real Bottleneck Is Moving Upstream

For decades, businesses have competed partly on their ability to execute.

Who can manufacture faster?

Who can hire more people?

Who can produce more content?

Who can process more transactions?

AI is changing the economics of execution.

But when execution becomes cheaper, another constraint becomes more important.

Deciding what should be executed in the first place.

I see five increasingly important stages of value creation:

Identifying the right problem.
Accessing reliable information and context.
Choosing the right solution.
Executing and verifying the result.
Connecting the result to a customer, transaction, or measurable business outcome.

AI can accelerate several of these stages.

But accelerating one stage does not automatically improve the entire system.

For example, an AI agent might generate a sophisticated market analysis in seconds.

But if the underlying data is outdated, the analysis is wrong.

If the analysis is correct but nobody makes a decision, it creates little operational value.

If the decision is correct but cannot reach customers, there may still be no economic return.

This is why I think the next competitive advantage will increasingly belong to organizations that can connect intelligence to execution.

Not simply organizations that own the most powerful AI models.

3. The Hidden Cost of AI Productivity

There is another problem that deserves attention.

AI does not eliminate all work.

Sometimes it changes where the work happens.

Consider a company that previously required two days to produce a research report.

With AI, the report can be generated in 20 minutes.

That sounds like an enormous productivity improvement.

But somebody still needs to:

Verify the information.
Check the assumptions.
Identify missing context.
Resolve conflicting evidence.
Decide whether the conclusions are reliable.
Take responsibility for the resulting decision.

In some situations, AI reduces the total workload.

In others, it simply moves the workload from production to verification.

And when AI generates more material than an organization can meaningfully evaluate, it can create a new bottleneck.

More information.

More recommendations.

More decisions.

More opportunities to make mistakes.

A recent November 2 report in The Washington Post described companies tracking employee AI usage, including token consumption and time spent using AI platforms.

Stanford researcher Arvind Karunakaran made an important observation: consuming more tokens does not necessarily create more business value.

I agree.

Measuring AI adoption through usage alone is like measuring a company's success by counting how many emails its employees send.

It tells us something about activity.

It tells us very little about whether the business is becoming better.

4. Why Some Companies Will Capture the AI Productivity Gains — And Others Won't

I think the next major separation in the business world will occur between companies that simply add AI to existing processes and companies that redesign their entire operating models around it.

These are fundamentally different strategies.

Company A: AI as an additional tool

It purchases subscriptions.

Employees use AI to write faster, summarize documents, and automate small tasks.

The existing organizational structure remains largely unchanged.

The company may become somewhat more efficient, but its fundamental economics remain similar.

Company B: AI as a redesigned operating system

It rethinks how work is organized.

It eliminates unnecessary handoffs.

It connects information across departments.

It automates repetitive decisions within defined boundaries.

It creates new services that were previously too expensive to offer.

It changes how customers are acquired, served, and retained.

The second company has a much greater opportunity to create structural advantages.

But even here, technology alone is insufficient.

A company needs reliable data, appropriate incentives, operational discipline, customer demand, and accountability.

This is why I would not automatically assume that the companies spending the most on AI will become the most profitable.

Spending is an input.

Productivity is an intermediate result.

Profitability is an economic outcome.

They are not interchangeable.

5. The Next Scarce Resource May Be Judgment

Here is the idea I find most interesting.

When information was expensive, people who possessed information had an advantage.

When software was expensive, people who could build software had an advantage.

When production was expensive, organizations with manufacturing capacity had an advantage.

But what happens when intelligence and production become increasingly accessible?

The advantage may shift toward people who can consistently make better decisions.

Not because AI cannot make decisions.

But because real-world decisions require more than generating plausible answers.

They require understanding:

Which problems are worth solving.
Which information deserves trust.
Which risks are acceptable.
Which opportunities have genuine demand.
Which results are actually sustainable.
When a seemingly attractive opportunity should be rejected.

I would add one important qualification.

Human judgment is not automatically a competitive advantage.

People can make poor decisions just as easily as machines can.

Judgment becomes valuable when it is supported by domain expertise, reliable evidence, feedback from real outcomes, and accountability.

The future advantage will not belong to someone who simply claims to have better intuition.

It will belong to people and organizations that can demonstrate better decisions over time.

6. What Should Investors Actually Measure?

This shift also changes how I think investors should evaluate AI companies.

Instead of asking only:

How many employees are using AI?

How many agents have been deployed?

How much money is being invested in AI?

I would start asking different questions.

Revenue quality

Is AI generating additional revenue, or simply replacing existing expenditure?

Productivity realization

Are time savings actually being converted into higher output, lower costs, or better customer experiences?

Unit economics

Is the cost of serving each additional customer declining after accounting for inference, infrastructure, human supervision, and support?

Customer retention

Are customers continuing to pay because the AI product solves an important problem?

Competitive durability

Can competitors reproduce the same functionality, or does the company possess proprietary data, distribution, integration, or customer relationships?

These questions matter because AI capabilities are spreading rapidly.

A feature that creates a temporary advantage today may become a standard feature tomorrow.

The lasting economic advantage may sit somewhere else.

It may be in customer relationships, distribution, proprietary information, workflow integration, or the ability to consistently deliver a trusted outcome.

7. The Most Important Question Is Not How Much AI a Company Uses

It is what the company can now accomplish that it could not economically accomplish before.

Stanford's 2026 AI Index estimates that organizational AI adoption reached 88% in its surveyed organizations.

Its research also estimates annual U.S. consumer surplus from generative AI at $172 billion by early 2026.

So there is clearly real value being created.

But consumer value and corporate profitability are different measurements.

A technology can be extremely useful to consumers while many businesses struggle to capture that value.

That distinction is important.

The companies that ultimately win may not be those that produce the most AI output.

They may be those that build the best economic systems around it.

And I suspect this will become increasingly visible as the market moves beyond experimentation and starts demanding measurable returns.

My Conclusion

I don't believe the AI revolution will be decided by who generates the most tokens, deploys the most agents, or produces the largest volume of content.

Those are measurements of technological activity.

The more important question is whether that activity creates something people genuinely value and are willing to pay for.

AI is making production cheaper.

But cheaper production does not automatically create demand, trust, distribution, or sustainable profits.

In fact, it may make those things more important.

When everyone can produce more, the ability to decide what matters becomes increasingly valuable.

That is the economic transition I want to understand.

And perhaps the biggest mistake businesses can make today is celebrating how much more they can produce without asking whether they are creating anything more valuable.

— Le Wang
Teraliq Quant
Independent Research | AI · Markets · Risk
Evidence over hype.

text:
Wow, I didn’t know about that! But I do know a story about orange groves, Walt Disney, Leslie Wexner, and New Albany that some people will find interesting…

Both Disneyland and New Albany relied on secrecy and intermediaries to quietly assemble large contiguous blocks of land from multiple small owners at controlled prices, enabling a single developer to control a major planned project.

—

Disney’s Disneyland site (Anaheim, 1950s)

After Stanford Research Institute (SRI) recommended the Anaheim area (along the Santa Ana Freeway) over Burbank based on factors like flat land, access, climate, and growth trends, Disney moved to acquire a roughly 160-acre quarter-section of orange groves plus surrounding parcels. Local realtors Ed Wagner and Frank Miller (recommended by Anaheim Chamber of Commerce figures) secured options and contracts from about 12–17 owners without revealing Disney as the buyer. This kept the process anonymous to prevent speculation, holdouts, and price inflation in a booming area; the land was delivered for roughly $640,000–$879,000 total (around $4,500+ per acre). Additional nearby orange ranches were bought, giving Disney control over the core site for the park.

—

Les Wexner’s New Albany, Ohio (mid-1980s onward)

Wexner (with developer Jack Kessler) targeted the small rural village of New Albany (then ~400–500 residents). Early purchases were made anonymously through third-party buyers such as the Smith and Hale law firm. Once a base was secured, they shifted to the New Albany Company (NACO), which they controlled, to assemble thousands of acres (reports cite figures in the 10,000-acre range over time). This allowed them to master-plan (based on Irvine) an upscale Georgian-style community with residential areas, golf courses, business parks, and infrastructure under unified control. Later expansions for tech sites (e.g., data centers, Intel) continued the pattern via subsidiaries/LLCs, sometimes with non-disclosure agreements and above-market offers.

—

Core similarities:

Anonymous intermediaries: Both used local agents, law firms, or third parties so sellers did not know a high-profile, well-funded buyer was assembling a large site. Once the buyer’s identity is known, prices typically jump and negotiations become harder.

Land aggregation for control: Each needed not just one plot but enough contiguous land to shape the surrounding environment and realize a grand vision (Disney’s theme park; Wexner’s planned enclave/town).

Cost and strategic control: Secrecy minimized premium prices during the assembly phase and reduced the risk of holdouts or fragmented development that could undermine the project.
The scale and later techniques differed (Disney’s Anaheim effort was smaller and more focused on a park; Wexner’s evolved into ongoing land-banking with corporate subsidiaries), and Disney’s later Florida Walt Disney World project used more elaborate shell companies. The Anaheim Disneyland case and New Albany, however, share the same foundational tactic of quiet, proxy-driven land assembly.

text:
1. “Only for the saved”
If someone is already saved and justified by faith in Christ, Scripture treats them as already clean and accepted. John 13:10, 1 Corinthians 6:11, and Ephesians 5:25–27 present the believer as washed and presented holy. Adding a required purifying process after death for the saved undercuts that present standing.

2. “We aren’t becoming sanctified by ourselves”
Agreed that sanctification is by grace. The issue is timing and location. The New Testament locates the ongoing work of the Spirit in this life (2 Corinthians 3:18; Philippians 2:12–13; Romans 8). It does not describe a post-death continuation of that process before entering the Lord’s presence.

3. “No official length of time”
The flexibility on duration doesn’t solve the core problem. Whether it lasts a moment or ages, the claim is still that something remains unfinished for the justified believer at death. The New Testament’s language of being “present with the Lord” at death (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23) and Jesus’ words to the thief (“today… paradise,” Luke 23:43) leave no room for an intervening state.

4. “It’s very old / prayers for the dead”
Early Christian practices and later tradition are real historical data, but they are not the same as apostolic doctrine. The New Testament never instructs believers to pray for the dead, offer sacrifices for them, or intercede to aid their purification. That silence is significant when the doctrine is presented as necessary for many of the saved.

5. “Not about earning heaven; God’s work of completing sanctification”
If heaven still requires a further completing work after death, then the believer does not enter on the basis of Christ’s finished work alone. Hebrews 10:10 and 10:14 say we have been sanctified once for all and perfected for all time by the one sacrifice. That language is hard to reconcile with a necessary post-mortem process.
6. “Not a mini-hell”

The tone can be softer than popular caricatures, but the substance remains: a justified person still needs purification before full entry into heaven. The New Testament’s consistent picture is that death for the believer means immediate presence with Christ, not a further painful or purifying stage.

7. “Praying for the dead is helpful”
Analogy to praying for the living doesn’t establish the practice. We have clear commands and examples for interceding for the living. We have none for the dead. Once a person has died in Christ, the biblical witness is that they are already with Him; further intercession to alter their state is not taught.

8. “Not separated from God”
This softens the older imagery, but it still places the believer in a state where full union and entry into heaven are delayed. Scripture’s comfort to the dying and grieving is that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord—not present with the Lord in a purifying waiting room.

9. “Doesn’t mean the cross was insufficient; deals with sanctification and temporal consequences”
Distinguishing justification from sanctification is right, and distinguishing eternal from temporal consequences has a biblical basis in this life. Extending that distinction into a necessary post-death process for the justified still treats Christ’s work as leaving a remaining debt or impurity that must be addressed before heaven. Hebrews 10 presents the sacrifice as having dealt with sins so thoroughly that no further offering is needed.

10. “Necessary for many; nothing unclean shall enter”
Revelation 21:27 is true. The Protestant reading is that those in Christ are already made clean by His blood and righteousness (Revelation 7:14; Ephesians 1:6–7). If residual attachment to sin at the moment of death still requires a further divine process before the believer can enter, then the righteousness credited in justification is not yet sufficient for heaven.

I really don't understand this.

I see many people now apply to @ycombnaitor with the app that they vibe-coded (some even with revenue).

It makes no sense to me - even if you get in, money won't save you- and this is why I never applied to YC with Postiz.

I would never invest in a vibe-coded app, and I got offers from startups making above $1m ARR (built pre-AI era, of course)

Don't get me wrong, it can make a lot of money (Postiz: $4.3m ARR), but the chances are slim.

Just build it yourself and get it to $10-$20k MRR.

When to apply to YC? When you have
- Deeptech startup
- Medical
- Security
- Infrastructure barrier (think Deel, Stripe, etc.)

This isn't to bum you. It's to save you.
If you raise a lot of money, you would have to make a lot more money- bottom-up is not an option anymore. You need Enterprise deals, and a lot.

You'll also be flooded with competitors because everyone can build what you build. So you will need to be reaaaallly good at marketing.

Your salary will be capped by investors, and in the end,  you'll most likely close your startup. Your risk of success becomes much, much lower.

Don't get me wrong, I am not the - you have to go bootstrap. I am not. My next company will most likely be VC-based.

After Postiz, when I am rich already, I don't care to sacrifice years of my life for VC and build something huge (not vibe-coded, of course), probably deep tech.

text:
The Anatomy of a Cultural Rebranding: Archival and Anthropological Reality Behind James P. Blair’s 1965 Portrait

​Before taking the boy in James P. Blair’s portrait on a biographical tour from Wollega to Assab and then to Tesseney, it is worth making one shorter journey first: to page 551 of the April 1965 issue of National Geographic. In “Ethiopian Adventure”, the magazine identifies Blair’s subject as a “Beni Amer boy of western Eritrea”. That is how the publication described him when the photograph appeared, six decades before your “Fun Facts” post.

● ​The Archival Trail and Circulation

​The Ethiopian Tourism Commission subsequently reproduced the portrait in its 13 Months of Sunshine series. The Smithsonian preserves a postcard from around 1970 bearing the printed caption “Beni Amer boy of northwestern Ethiopia”.

​The geographical wording changed between the magazine and the postcard. The identification Beni Amer remained. Indeed, the Ethiopian institution that promoted the image used precisely the designation your post leaves unexplained. The postcard documents how the portrait circulated. Even a hundred calendars bearing the same smile would tell us little about where the boy was born.

​There is also a published source for the name you give. In September 2026, Kidane Shimendi identified the boy as Omar Muhammad Idris Haji Ali Goret in an article published by Eritrea’s Ministry of Information. Shimendi places the photographic encounter in Tesseney and describes Omar as a boy at the time. Your post says he moved there as an adult. A childhood visit and a later move are perfectly compatible, but the distinction matters.

​Which source dates the move? And which source identifies Wollega as his birthplace, records his Oromo ancestry, or places his father at the Assab naval station? Shimendi’s article supplies none of those details.

● ​The "Re-Branding" Absurdity

​Your post asserts he was "well known as Beni-Amer." Beni-Amer is not an artistic pseudonym or military handle; it is a centuries-old endogamous confederation with established lineages and distinct languages (predominantly Tigre and Bedawie). One does not simply wake up in Wollega and adopt Beni-Amer kinship on a whim.

● ​Anthropological Forensics: The Marks on the Face

​The human face in pastoralist societies is an open cultural map. Here, every marking points toward the western lowlands and eastern Sudan, not the Oromo highlands:

° ​The Incisions (Shallukh / Wasm):

 The subject exhibits sharp, deliberate linear incisions at the temples and upper cheeks. Across Beja, Tigre, and neighboring Sahelian groups, these marks serve two functions: clan identification and therapeutic bloodletting to treat childhood eye ailments or fevers.

° ​The Oromo Contrast: While Oromo society possesses rich symbolic traditions governed by the Gadaa system, this Sahelian scarification does not exist in Wollega culture. Claiming these temple cuts represent an Oromo youth is akin to calling Viking runes Venetian lace.

​Evidentiary Standards

​A recorded family interview, a birth record linked to Omar, or a service document identifying his father could materially strengthen your account. The post offers readers no way to trace it to any such source.

​So, Habtish, the Beni-Amer identification has a publication, a date and a page number. What is the source for the Wollega–Assab account? Produce it, and readers can assess it on its merits. Until then, the two exclamation marks after “Fun Facts” are doing rather more work than the footnotes.

#BeniAmer #EritreanHeritage #EritreanHistory #JamesPBlair #NationalGeographic #HistoricalEvidence #PhotographicHistory #CulturalIdentity #FactsMatter #PreserveOurHistory

text:
My dear Col Sushil, you know very well that every issue has two sides, just like a coin. Rather than looking at the Agnipath Scheme only through the lens of criticism, we should also consider its potential benefits and long-term opportunities.

Having seen the Army closely, you would appreciate that many young men join the forces with immense talent, ambition and potential. Some even aspire to become commissioned officers but, due to financial constraints or other circumstances, cannot pursue their dream of cracking the UPSC & many more examination. A structured four-year service opportunity can give such youngsters valuable exposure, discipline, confidence and a platform to fulfil their aspirations.

Secondly, those who wish to pursue a commission can continue to work towards that goal through the established selection processes, just as many serving personnel have done in the past.

Thirdly, after four years, those who transition out can explore opportunities in state government services and other sectors, where their military training, discipline and experience can be valuable assets. In many cases, these careers may also offer a more settled lifestyle.

My point is simple: we should not judge the scheme solely by its challenges or implementation gaps. Constructive criticism is necessary, particularly when national security is involved, but so is an objective assessment of its potential. The real question should be how to make the scheme more effective, transparent and beneficial for both the armed forces and the youth.

Reforms may be necessary, but dismissing the entire idea without considering its positive dimensions would not be fair either.

text:
Tell a Japanese person "Fuck you," and there's a good chance they'll be fascinated.

A Japanese man's story about exactly that has 27 million views in Japan right now. Cursed at by a stranger as a teen in America, he asked for one more, because he'd only ever heard it in movies.

Japanese people loved it, because we get it. Japanese barely has real swear words. Our harshest everyday insult is basically "idiot."

So how do Japanese people actually hurt each other?

We get more polite.

In Kyoto, the old capital, the story goes that if your host offers you a bowl of rice with tea, it means it's time to go home. If they compliment your watch, you've stayed too long. If a neighbor says your kid's piano playing has really improved, they mean it's too loud.

No curse words required.

That's why "Fuck you" sounds almost friendly to us. At least you know where you stand.

In Japan, the words that really hurt sound like kindness.

text:
The Dravidar Kazhagam has been criticising #DMK General Secretary @katpadidmk following reports that Sanskrit mantras were chanted during a wedding ceremony in his family. While I may have a thousand political criticisms of him, I am making this post with the understanding that this was a private family occasion.

I could have criticised them for corruption, for allegedly siphoning off public money, and I have done so and will continue to do so. I have also questioned the arrangements made for family functions of political leaders, including those from other parties, because of the public conduct of certain individuals associated with such events. However, neither I nor anyone else has the authority to dictate how someone should conduct their family functions.

Neither Duraimurugan nor his family has ever publicly claimed that they do not believe in God. Politics is one thing, while personal beliefs and family occasions are entirely different matters. They have their own respect for Siddhars and Rishis. They have deep devotion towards Shirdi Sai Baba, and they believe that their prosperity in life is due to the blessings of Lord Venkateswara of Tirupati. These are personal beliefs that exist beyond the boundaries of politics.

Being in politics does not mean that someone must conduct their family functions according to the preferences of political critics. Attempts to drag politics into private family occasions and dictate how they should be conducted deserve to be condemned. They may have committed political mistakes, and I have no disagreement with those who criticise them on political grounds. But mocking or ridiculing someone's personal faith because of their political affiliation is simply unacceptable.

The Karunanidhi family has always had individuals with strong religious beliefs. It is often said that Karunanidhi himself was not a believer. But how many know that he would occasionally offer prayers to the Vinayagar at the temple near his residence while passing by? Dayalu Ammal and Selvi Akka are deeply religious. I have personally seen them visit the Anjaneyar temple on several occasions. I have also accompanied one of them to the Adi Kumbeswarar Temple in Kumbakonam. And does anyone seriously believe that Durga Stalin lacks spiritual devotion?

While the party leadership politically projects opposition to Hinduism, a considerable number of its second rung leaders regularly visit temples and Siddhar Peetams. This is not something exclusive to the DMK. Leaders across several political parties and organisations that publicly position themselves against Hinduism continue to practise their personal faith. This is somewhat similar to their stand on Hindi. While publicly opposing Hindi imposition, some of the very same leaders teach Hindi as a third language in the schools and colleges they run.

The real problem here is the inability of these leaders to question their own party leadership when it takes an aggressive anti Hindu position. Their reluctance to speak up against the leadership is what ultimately exposes them to such criticism and ridicule.

text:
please help Respected Sir, Subject: Urgent appeal to protect the lives, homes and lifelong savings of nearly 3,000 residents of PWS, 7 Hills Apartments, from the proposed 100-foot road widening—Kokapet, Narsingi I write with deep pain and anxiety as a retired professor and a resident of Power Welfare Society (PWS), 7 Hills Apartments, Kokapet, Narsingi, Hyderabad. The proposed 100-foot road adjoining our society has left us frightened about the safety of our buildings, the future of our homes and the security of nearly 3,000 residents. I respectfully seek your immediate intervention before any action causes damage that cannot be undone. PWS was registered in 2005 under the Andhra Pradesh Societies Act by employees of the Central Power Sector. Its housing project was launched on 1 June 2009 and comprises seven high-rise towers with 853 apartments. Many families invested their lifelong earnings and retirement savings here, trusting the validity of the land documents and the approvals under which the project was built. For about 15 years, the society has been paying municipal taxes, water charges and other applicable charges. We believed that a lawfully established home would offer us peace and security in our later years. Large residential projects have since come up, or are being developed, around our society. We understand that a notification has been issued requiring PWS and neighbouring landowners to surrender land for a proposed 100-foot road. Municipal personnel have begun marking the affected areas. The proposed alignment appears to affect our society from both the front (RR Corp)  and the rear (Alekya Homes). Residents are deeply concerned that an established community is being made to bear a severe burden to meet the access needs of surrounding developments. According to our present understanding of the markings and proposed alignment, the affected area includes land close to or beneath parts of our buildings and basement parking. Residents fear that more than 100 parking spaces could be lost when the impact on both sides is considered. Our Lord Ganesha temple, electrical installation serving the apartments, part of the children’s park and many mature trees also appear to be at risk. The extent of the impact must be established through an official joint survey and clearly explained to every affected resident. Our gravest concern is the safety of the towers, particularly F, E and A/B blocks. Any cutting into or excavation near a shared basement or building foundation raises serious questions about structural stability. Residents also need clear answers about fire-engine access, emergency evacuation, electricity supply and safe movement within the society. These concerns require an independent assessment by qualified structural and fire-safety experts before any demolition, excavation or removal takes place. For us, this is a potential threat to human life. I live in Flat 102, F Block, having invested my hard-earned post-retirement savings in this home. At this stage of life, the fear of losing the safety of my home is deeply distressing. A home holds a family’s memories, a lifetime of sacrifice and the hope of spending one’s remaining years with dignity. It is painful to feel that everything we worked for could be placed at risk by a decision over which we have little control. Many of our neighbours are retired power-sector employees who spent their working lives serving the country. There are elderly residents, children and families who depend on this community for security and support. The continued marking exercise has created fear and uncertainty. We worry about what may happen next and whether our concerns will be heard before machinery arrives. No family should have to live with such anxiety inside its own home. A wide road running close to our buildings on both sides would also expose residents to traffic, noise, dust and loss of privacy. Children’s play areas and the green spaces that make the society liveable could be reduced. The loss of basement parking could create further congestion and obstruct movement within the premises. These consequences deserve a careful assessment alongside the proposed road’s benefits. We recognise the need for better roads and planned development. But development must protect the people who already live in an area. It would be deeply unjust if the needs of new projects were met by placing established homes and residents’ safety at risk. We request a transparent explanation of why this alignment was chosen, what alternatives were examined and how the burden on existing communities was considered. Our concern about possible undue influence should be examined impartially, on the basis of records and evidence. We understand that neighbouring landowners, including Tera Nagarjuna Reddy and others, have approached the Hon’ble High Court of Telangana in Writ Petition No. 32694 of 2026, CNR No. HBHC010671982026. We have been informed that directions concerning due process and maintenance of status quo have been issued. I request the authorities to examine the actual order, clarify its scope and comply strictly with every applicable direction. The continuing marking activity has increased residents’ anxiety, and we seek a written explanation of its purpose and the action proposed. I respectfully request that you direct an immediate pause on any demolition, excavation, taking possession or alteration affecting PWS until the residents’ objections, the relevant court directions and the safety implications have been examined. Please arrange a joint site inspection with society representatives and independent experts. We also request copies of the notification, the approved road alignment, the survey showing the exact land affected and the technical reports relied upon. Residents should be given a meaningful opportunity to present their concerns and receive a reasoned written response. Above all, please examine an alternative alignment that protects our occupied buildings, shared basements, essential facilities and community spaces. Our homes must not be treated as expendable simply because they stand in the path of a proposed road. The responsibility of the authorities is to find a solution that serves the public without placing an existing community in danger. No compensation can remove our agony. No amount of money can restore the peace of an elderly person who fears that the home built with a lifetime’s savings may become unsafe. Nor can it replace the security, memories and bonds that hold this community together. Our appeal is for the preservation of our homes and the protection of our lives. Our society has limited funds to sustain a prolonged legal battle. That should not make our voices less worthy of being heard. We seek fair treatment, transparent decisions and protection of our lives and homes. We are determined to pursue every peaceful and lawful means available to us. We will fight till the end to protect our homes, our dignity and the safety of our families. Sir, please treat this as an urgent appeal from a resident whose peace of mind and retirement security are at stake. Behind every affected flat is a family. Behind every retirement investment are decades of work and sacrifice. I request your personal intervention, a written assurance that residents’ safety will be protected and an early meeting with our society representatives. Please do not allow our remaining years to be consumed by fear and a struggle to save the homes we worked all our lives to secure. Act before an avoidable loss becomes an irreversible tragedy. We place our hope in your sense of justice and your duty to protect the people. Yours faithfully, Dr. V. S. P. text:
It was on the radio, 10 mins prior. You can find the audio. ATC offered them a route around. The captain made a slight deviation because it wasn't serious and they were above the storm until that cell ballooned up from 33000 ft to 48000 ft ceiling in a few minutes and by then it was too late for them to climb out of it.
From grok:
The earlier ATC exchange you’re remembering does exist. It comes from Miami Center (ZMA) LiveATC archives and covers the period roughly 10–15 minutes before the final mayday (around 12:36–12:37 p.m. EST while the jet was still ~80 miles / ~8 minutes from the cell it later entered). It is not in the short final-minute clips that circulate most widely, but it appears in longer reconstructions and analyses (especially MyRadar/Matthew Cappucci’s weather note and some YouTube breakdowns that pull the earlier sector recordings).
Key excerpts from the earlier exchange (paraphrased/transcribed from public LiveATC-based sources)
Around the time the jet was descending from FL410 toward FL350 and crossing into Florida airspace:
ATC cleared N722BD direct to Freeport and warned that the turn/route “looks pretty nasty.”
Controller described a large area of moderate-to-extreme precipitation (roughly 100 miles in diameter, reported in the 11 o’clock position ~25 miles ahead in one reconstruction).
Crew (captain’s voice in the analysis) said something to the effect of “[we] may need a slight left deviation for that weather up ahead.”
ATC approved weather deviations: “deviations left and right are approved… Freeport when able.”
The aircraft took a left deviation. At that point they were still well clear of the specific rapidly growing cell they later entered near Royal Palm Beach/Wellington.
MyRadar’s summary of the same period (Matthew Cappucci) states exactly this sequence and notes the storm cell was still building dramatically (tops rising from ~33,000 ft to ~48,000 ft in ~20 minutes). The crew continued after the advisory and deviation approval rather than requesting a major reroute farther north or south.
Later (starting ~12:45–12:47 p.m., now at FL350 and closer to the cell), the familiar short segment begins:
Light clear ice (manageable), moderate turbulence (±600–700 ft), OAT –47 °C, direct Freeport.
Request for a better ride.
ATC: ride should improve in their airspace; better rides ahead.
Crew: now picking up precipitation; request climb to FL370 (approved).
Within ~20–30 seconds: mayday, descending 8–10k then 20k+ fpm, overspeed, 60° bank, “we’re going to crash into the ground,” “out of time.”
Where to find the audio
YouTube searches for “N722BD ATC” or “Full ATC Audio Learjet Final 5 Minutes” (e.g., the InterTainment video covering ~5 min 48 s of Miami Center, and VASAviation’s weather-focused edit). Some of these include or reference the earlier deviation/“pretty nasty” portion.
https://t.co/tYrZZmE8tv archives for Miami Center (ZMA) frequencies around 17:30–17:50 UTC on 1 Nov 2026. The final segment is on ~125.325 MHz; the earlier weather/deviation talk was on a prior sector.
Detailed weather + ATC timeline: MyRadar MetNote on N722BD (Matthew Cappucci).
No official NTSB transcript has been released yet—these are reconstructions from public LiveATC recordings. The audio of the final minute is widely available but extremely distressing; the earlier portion is calmer but still relevant to the weather-avoidance decisions.

What a Monumental night with Elegant, Cassy, and Heavy with #History. An Honor to stand in the presence of 40 years of Rap-A-Lot’s independent reign.

Mid 1994. Shortly after Domino’s album drop the one I was featured on. I’m in a Sherman Oaks studio with @djbattlecat. He’s running a showcase, scouting new Artists. I’m not there for that. I’m there to finish a joint we started earlier. He heads into the showcase, tells me to hold Studio B and stay working. I pull up, he plays the beat back, looks at me and says, “You gonna let these other cats rap to this, or you gonna do what you do?” The song wasn’t finished. He didn’t care. “Rap exactly what you rapped to me earlier.”

I stepped in the Booth 🎤 and did just that.

When I walked back into the Control room, the energy shifted. #BattleCat was lit. Labels started circling. One of them stepped up in a #RapALot tee and hat, Fifth Ward tilt sharp. Introduced himself as J. Asked if I was signed. I was a free agent with a few offers already on the table. He handed me a card. No title. No “CEO.” Just “James Smith, Rap-A-Lot.”

I was ready to bounce. The crowd wasn’t why I came. Before I left, he asked if I was down for breakfast the next morning. Sit at a table, chop it up. I said yeah.

Next day he pulls up. 🤲🏾 Seagram’s 🕊️ in the car Bay Area legend I already knew personally ( Rest In Peace ). Whole ride I still don’t know who this man from #Texas really is. We get to Roscoe’s on Pico. He steps to the restroom. #Seagram looks at me and says, “You know who that is?” I said yeah, a Rap-A-Lot A&R or something. Seagram said, “Nah, N🥷GGA. That’s the Owner. James Prince.”@jprincerespect 🎩

We sat and had a real #Business meeting over Chicken and Waffles. He knew my history. Said he was building Rap-A-Lot West and wanted me in on it helping find talent, helping shape it. That Breakfast was the beginning of the mentorship, the deal, and everything that followed.

Full story in the book:

text:
Send your cold email to Claude with this prompt:

You'll get it graded against the checks behind $70M+ in pipeline, then rewritten 3 ways

Thank me later ↓

<inputs> Ask me for: the email (subject, body, PS and follow up), who it goes to (industry, title, company size), what I sell and the result it gets, my best client result with real numbers, and the inboxes I'm sending to (mostly Google, mostly Microsoft, or a mix). </inputs> <direction> Grade my email the way a team that has sent 10M+ cold emails would. Judge the offer first, then the targeting, and the copy last. A great offer with average copy beats great copy with a weak offer. The email has 1 job: get a reply from someone who has never heard of me. It reads like I'm emailing a coworker. Plain text, short sentences, zero filler. Banned: "I hope this finds you well", "I noticed you", compliments about their college or their latest post, links in the body (write company(.)com instead), images, open tracking, unsubscribe links, the first name in the subject line, "Got 15 minutes?", selling the mechanism instead of the outcome, and social proof in the body. </direction> <scorecard> Score each check from 0 to 10, quote the exact line that lost points, and say how to fix it: - Offer: a free front end offer they'd want even if they never buy (an audit, a teardown, a sample, a free campaign, a mock-up of their product) - Relevance: a pain at their level, in their industry's own words - Specificity: the value prop is a number ("$4/sq ft savings on concrete moisture issues") instead of a claim ("we help reduce flooring costs") - Opener: line 1 is a question about their world, and the email talks about them before it talks about me - CTA: a soft permission ask ("Mind if I share it?") they can answer in 1 word - Proof: a company at their level, from their industry, sitting in the PS - Length: under 65 words in total, under 40 if they're on Microsoft, with 45 as the target - Subject: 1 to 3 lowercase words, with no punctuation - Spam risk: big numbers like 100,000, links, spam words, anything that reads like a newsletter - Personalization: every variable earns its place, so {PROJECT} or {COMPETITOR} stays and "saw you went to UCLA" goes The email passes 8 of these 10 before it goes out. </scorecard> <rewrite> Then rewrite it 3 ways, every version under 65 words: - Version A, the one line offer: "{first_name} - interested in {free front end offer} for {company_name}?" Then my signature, and a PS with the proof. - Version B, question first: a question about their world, the value asset, then the soft permission ask. - Version C, the case study: a client from their industry, the result with a timeframe, then the free offer. Spintax every 3 to 5 words in all 3 versions, with 3 options for each subject line. End each one with a written opt out and a spintaxed keyword: "If you'd rather not hear from me, just reply {banana|peanut|bird} and I'll stop." Write 1 follow up and only 1. It's shorter than the first email and brings something new, like a second result or a sample. </rewrite> <gotchas> If my offer is weak, tell me straight away, before touching the copy, because a rewrite can't fix a bad offer. Every rewrite stays the same length as my original or shorter. For enterprise buyers, keep it consultative: the exact role instead of a department, no hard sell, and the opener "are you the best person to speak to about {topic} at {company}?" Keep 1 version with zero AI personalization, so I can test it against the rest. </gotchas> <start> Ask me for the inputs, score the email, then show me the 3 rewrites side by side with the word count under each. </start>

text:
Between December 1884 and December 1885, eight people were murdered in Austin, Texas, and several others were badly injured. Most of the victims were Black women who worked as live-in servants. They were attacked indoors while asleep, usually with an axe.

The first killing, on 30 December 1884, was of Mollie Smith. The attacks continued through the following spring and summer: Eliza Shelly, Irene Cross, eleven-year-old Mary Ramey, and Gracie Vance, who was killed alongside Orange Washington. On Christmas Eve 1885, two white women, Susan Hancock and Eula Phillips, were killed within about an hour of each other in different parts of the city.

Austin panicked. Patrols and vigilance committees formed, rewards were offered, and dozens of men were arrested, most of them Black. Two husbands were charged over the Christmas Eve killings; one conviction was overturned, and the other man was not convicted. The attacks then stopped.

The writer O. Henry, then living in Austin, used the phrase servant girl annihilators in a private letter, and the name attached itself to the case long afterward. It was never solved. Modern researchers have proposed suspects, but no identification has been established. 

Historical photos that will send chills down your spine: https://t.co/5nIVtOBX72

text:
WHY SANCTIONS ARE A HEADLINE FOR CRITICS AND A SHRUG IN KIGALI

              By Ubukungu Talks | 03 November 2026

A WORD TO THE CITIZEN

Every time Washington announces another sanctions round, two reactions appear within hours. Critics and exiled opposition voices treat it as proof of a country in trouble. Official Kigali answers with quiet confidence and a familiar line about security. Ordinary Rwandans in between are left asking which version to believe, and whether any of it will reach their wallet.

Why do sanctions look so different from the two sides, how much can Rwanda really absorb, and where does the confidence end?

I. TWO AUDIENCES, TWO READINGS

For critics, sanctions are validation. They arrive from a powerful capital, they carry official language about support for M23, and they fit a story the critics have told for years. That is why they travel so far in international and diaspora media.

For the government, the same news is an external opinion, one it publicly rejects. After the March 2026 sanctions on the Rwanda Defence Force, it called the measures unjust and one-sided. Its position is that national security comes first and that its concerns about the FDLR have not been addressed.

Inside Rwanda there is a third reason the story looks small. Sanctions on a ministry and a savings society do not change the price of beans this week. Press-freedom groups describe Rwanda’s media space as restrictive, a view the government disputes, and either way, public debate on this topic is limited. So a story that dominates foreign headlines can feel distant at home.

Calm in public does not tell us what is happening in private. What we can observe is behaviour, and the behaviour is that Rwanda has spent years preparing for exactly this kind of pressure.

II. WHAT RWANDA CAN ABSORB, IN NUMBERS

The strongest evidence is how different Rwanda’s finances look today.

Aid dependence has fallen sharply. When donors suspended aid in 2012, Rwanda relied on donors for about 40 percent of its budget. In the 2026/27 budget of Rwf 7.8 trillion, foreign grants are projected at about 7 percent, while domestic revenue covers about 68 percent and tax revenue alone accounts for 56.8 percent of financing. A government that does not need a donor’s grant is harder to pressure with one.

Direct trade with the United States is small. In the first quarter of 2025, Rwanda’s top export destinations were the UAE ($288.75 million), the DRC ($54.96 million), China ($23.45 million), Luxembourg ($11.98 million) and the United States ($10.73 million). Rwanda’s main import sources are China, Tanzania, Kenya, India and the UAE. A country whose trade runs through the Gulf, China, East Africa and India has little exposed to a US trade measure.

Growth has stayed strong. The IMF reports 9.7 percent growth in the first half of 2026 and projects 7.8 percent for the year, and Rwanda met all its measurable programme targets for end-June.

The 2012 precedent also helps the optimists. In July and August 2012, the US, the African Development Bank, the UK, Germany and Sweden withheld about $128.1 million in budget support over allegations about M23. The IMF reported Rwanda still grew 8 percent in 2012, and the government adjusted by re-phasing spending and preparing a supplementary budget. Within months, Germany unfroze some aid.

So the claim that Rwanda can take a hit is not just rhetoric. It rests on structural change.

III. WHAT “ABSORB” DOES NOT MEAN

Honesty requires the other half.

The 2012 shock still cost something. Growth in 2013 came in at 6.6 percent, against a projected 7.5 percent, and services growth slowed sharply. Private sector credit growth fell from 35 percent in 2012 to 10 percent in 2013, though the finance minister said aid cuts, weaker agriculture and high interest rates all contributed. The lesson is that Rwanda absorbed the shock but not for free.

Loans have replaced grants. Grants may be only 7 percent of the budget, but external loans are projected at 25.3 percent. Lenders are more sensitive to risk perception than donors are. The US is the largest single shareholder in both the IMF and World Bank, and I am not claiming any sanction on those institutions is planned. The point is that the exposure has shifted from “who gives us aid” to “who lends to us, and at what price.”

Exports are already under strain. Domestic exports fell 35.64 percent year on year in the second quarter of 2025, and UAE purchases dropped from over $288 million in Q2 2024 to $97.9 million. The data does not tell us why, and I will not attribute it to sanctions. But it shows how exposed a few buyers make Rwanda.

Prices are hurting now. Inflation reached 15.7 percent in August, against a central bank target of 5 percent, which the IMF links mainly to higher oil and fertiliser prices. That is not a sanctions effect, but it means households have less cushion for any additional shock.

Dollar plumbing is the weak point. Sanctions bite through the dollar system, not through trade. The 28 October action blocks property of the Ministry of Defence and Zigama within US reach and covers entities they own 50 percent or more. Banks that over-comply can create friction well beyond the two named institutions.

So the accurate summary is: Rwanda can absorb this round, but its capacity is built on growth, reserves and IMF support, all of which are strong today and none of which is permanent.

IV. WHY SECURITY RESONATES AT HOME

Part of the calm in Kigali comes from a political reality outside economics. Many Rwandans experience security as the foundation of everything else, and it is difficult to understand the national mood without the memory of 1994.

The numbers reflect that. The Rwanda Governance Scorecard’s safety and security pillar scored 90.15 percent in the 13th edition released on 22 October 2026. A separate Gallup survey found 78 percent of Rwandan adults feel safe walking alone at night, ahead of the UK at 76 percent and the US at 71 percent.

Two cautions are fair. The scorecard is produced by a government body, the Rwanda Governance Board, so it should be read alongside independent measures like Gallup. And critics argue that a security-first message can narrow space for debate. Both sides can be heard.

Now the part that matters for the citizen. The same scorecard shows quality of service delivery falling 3.25 points to 68.48 percent. In the 12th edition, citizens’ welfare scored 64.69 percent. In other words, Rwandans rate security far above services and welfare. Security is where the government’s credibility is strongest, but the daily cost of living is where patience is thinnest. A government can win the argument on national security and still lose goodwill on the price of cooking oil. That gap is the real political and economic risk of a long confrontation.

V. WHAT HISTORY ACTUALLY SAYS ABOUT SANCTIONS

A popular argument says that every country the US sanctioned ended up fine, or even better off. The evidence is more interesting than that, and it is mixed.

The most-cited research, the Peterson Institute’s study of 204 sanctions episodes, found that sanctions contributed to at least partial success in about one-third of cases. One of its authors, Gary Hufbauer, has said that sanctions over the last four to five decades typically cost the target less than two percent of GDP, with exceptions such as Iran, about five percent before the 2015 nuclear deal. Rhodesia’s economy lost over ten percent in the 1970s.

Two other findings matter for Rwanda. Success is more likely when the sender and target had friendly relations before sanctions: 46 percent for cordial relations versus 18 percent for antagonistic ones. And success depends on regime type: 27 percent for autocracies, 34 percent for anocracies and 47 percent for democracies. Whatever label anyone gives Rwanda, the finding is that determined governments often outlast sanctions.

But the data also warns against celebrating. Cuba has lived under a US embargo for over six decades. Venezuela’s economy shrank dramatically after 2013, and economists divide the blame between domestic policy and sanctions. A government that “survives” sanctions may still leave its citizens poorer. Survival is not the same as prosperity. And the fact that Rwanda was a close US partner until recently means, by the research, that this is precisely the kind of relationship in which US pressure tends to be taken more seriously.

So the honest reading: sanctions rarely force a country to change course quickly, and rarely collapse it, but they can leave a long drag on growth, financing and confidence, particularly for countries that depend on trust.

VI. “FRIEND OR ENEMY”: TESTING THE ARGUMENT

A view widely heard across Africa and beyond says that being an American friend can be as dangerous as being an enemy, and that Washington’s role as global enforcer is losing its fear factor. It deserves a fair test.

Supporters of the view point to partners that felt abandoned when US priorities changed, and to a world where China, the Gulf and India offer alternatives. Rwanda’s own trade data supports the second half: its biggest markets and suppliers are not American.

Critics of the view point out that many US partners, from South Korea and Japan to Poland, prospered inside the American security and financial system, and that the dollar’s reach has not weakened in practice. Where Washington can still hurt is finance, not trade.

My reading is that the lesson for Rwanda is not about choosing a camp. It is about optionality. A small country is safest when no single capital can decide its fate. Rwanda’s diversification toward the Gulf, China, India and East Africa is a sensible hedge. But hedging has limits when your bank still clears dollars and your IMF programme depends on global goodwill.

VII. WHAT A RWANDA-FIRST RESPONSE LOOKS LIKE

Keep growing the domestic base. The shift from 40 percent aid dependence to 7 percent grants is Rwanda’s best defence. Protect it by continuing to raise tax revenue and manage the debt carefully.

Treat inflation as the priority. If sanctions are a quiet risk, 15.7 percent inflation is a loud one. Households will judge the state on prices.

Protect the payment system. Authorities and banks should clarify what is and is not restricted, so that over-compliance does not freeze lawful business, and Zigama’s members and savers know where they stand.

Diversify buyers. A fall in sales to one major market, as the UAE figures show, can hurt more than any foreign measure.

Close the welfare gap. If security scores 90 percent and welfare scores 65 percent, that difference is the most important number in national politics.

Show a path forward. Citizens can accept a hard security line more readily when they are told what it costs and what would let it end.

VIII. WHAT TO WATCH

Whether payment frictions spread beyond the two designated entities. Whether borrowing costs rise. Whether the IMF Board approves the first review in December and what it says about inflation. Whether export markets recover. Whether donors who resumed support in the past stay engaged. And whether Kigali and Washington find a diplomatic way back before another round.

CONCLUSION

The fair summary is that sanctions are a headline for critics and a shrug in Kigali for good reasons: Rwanda’s budget depends on donors far less than before, its trade barely touches the US, its growth is strong, and its citizens place a very high value on security.

But a shrug is not a strategy. The cost of a long confrontation arrives slowly, through financing, prices, confidence and opportunity, and it is paid by ordinary households long before it shows up in official statistics. A country can be strong enough to survive pressure and still be poorer for enduring it.

Rwanda has shown that it can absorb. The harder question is what it is absorbing for, and for how long.

SUPPORT INDEPENDENT ANALYSIS

If you value independent, evidence-led analysis that connects geopolitics to jobs, prices and household welfare in Rwanda, consider supporting Ubukungu Talks on Buy Me a Coffee. Share the article, and keep the debate grounded in evidence.

2. Rwanda Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning, 2026/27 budget statement, 11 June 2026; UNICEF Rwanda budget brief 2026-2027

6. Rwanda Governance Board, Rwanda Governance Scorecard, 13th edition, 22 October 2026; Gallup Global Safety Report 2025

@norbertjmichel “Never Truly Private” gets some of the history right. Fannie and Freddie had federal charters and special privileges, and the market believed Washington stood behind them. But the case for abolishing them depends on leaving out key numbers. Here are the holes, using his figures where possible.

1. THE SWEEP IS MISSING
He says each PSPA amendment gave the companies MORE support. The August 2012 amendment took their entire net worth each quarter. A jury found that this breached the implied covenant owed to shareholders, the D.C. Circuit unanimously affirmed in July 2026, and rehearing was denied in October with no dissent. The judgment is about $812M. Collins upheld FHFA’s authority under the statute, but the court held that isn’t the same question as shareholders’ reasonable expectations. A paper on the conservatorship never mentions the sweep, Collins, or Fairholme.
2. NO NETTING OF THE “BAILOUT”
Treasury’s draws were about $191B. Dividends paid to Treasury were $301B, per FHFA’s own table. The PSPA doesn’t count those dividends as repayment, and that’s a fair legal point. But a reader of this paper would never learn the money went back at all.
3. “PRIVATIZES PROFITS WHILE SOCIALIZING LOSSES”
Private shareholders haven’t received a dividend since 2008. Treasury took the profits. That’s close to the opposite of what he describes for the last 18 years.
4. THE LOSSES
He cites $250B+ in losses by 2012 without asking what they were. Former Fannie CFO Tim Howard attributes $151B of the $187B drawn by then to noncash expenses booked by the conservator, and notes the companies later paid Treasury $158B in just 18 months. You can argue with his accounting, but you can’t just skip it.
5. “NEGATIVE CAPITAL”
He says both companies still have negative capital balances. Combined net worth was $200.6B at 9/30/26. CET1 is negative largely because the $193.4B senior preferred is excluded. The real debate is whether that stock should exist after $301B in payments. They’d still fall short of their ERCF requirements without it, so make that argument and show the math.
6. THE CRISIS CAUSE
He puts the GSEs at the heart of 2008, citing $700B of private subprime MBS, about 30% of issuance. By his own number, about 70% was bought by someone else. He also gives their mortgage share rising through 2003, then skips the private-label boom that followed. Howard’s figures: 2008-15 GSE single-family loss rates averaged under 50 bp a year, about a third of comparable bank-held loans and under a fifth of private-label.
7. WHO MISLED WHOM
FHFA sued 18 institutions in 2011 over private-label securities sold to the GSEs in 2005-07, alleging misrepresentation and in some cases fraud. It recovered $24.9B in settlements. That doesn’t clear the GSEs for buying the paper, but it belongs in any honest account of those purchases.
8. THE $3 TRILLION
He counts Fed MBS purchases as support for the GSEs. The Fed said it was supporting mortgage lending, housing markets, and the recovery. That’s monetary policy aimed at the mortgage market, and it would have helped any holder of those securities. It isn’t a cost of bailing out two companies. His own total also runs through 2019, more than a decade after the crisis.
9. “MULTIPLE BAILOUTS”
His main pre-2008 example is the 1980s. By his own description, that was regulatory forbearance and a tax provision, not a cash rescue.
10. WEAK EVIDENCE
His international rate comparison relies on Global Property Guide and Numbeo, with no adjustment for what a prepayable 30-year fixed provides compared with shorter-reset foreign loans. His volatility data ends in 2009. His $7.8T guarantee figure links to an op-ed.
11. NO TRANSITION
“Private markets work” isn’t a plan. What happens to $7.8T of guaranteed mortgages, the TBA market, and the 30-year fixed? What happens to spreads and mortgage rates? Private-label shut down after 2008, and only in 2025 did its quarterly issuance reach the highest level since 2007. He says there is no market failure and puts the burden of proof on the other side, then offers no numbers on any of this.

“Abolish the GSEs” is a statement of belief. Belief doesn’t need numbers, but a policy paper does.

text:
I found my missing dog in my ex-girlfriend’s engagement photos.

She’d helped me share the missing posters.

For eleven months, I thought somebody might have found him. Or that he was still out there somewhere, waiting for me to get close enough to hear him bark.

His name was Duke.

After the breakup, I moved out of our apartment. My new place wouldn’t be ready until Friday, so a friend offered to keep him for four nights.

On Wednesday afternoon, Duke disappeared from his fenced backyard.

My friend called me at work.

We searched until dark, then kept going with flashlights.

Over the next few weeks, I called shelters, checked found-dog posts, and drove out to look at dogs that barely resembled him.

My ex texted, “I’m so sorry. I know how much he means to you.”

She shared my post.

I thanked her.

Eventually, the calls stopped coming. I moved into the new place with his bed and no dog to put in it.

Then an acquaintance sent me a screenshot.

“Isn’t this Duke?”

My ex and a man were sitting on a picnic blanket, holding up her engagement ring.

Between them lay a black and tan dog.

I zoomed in on his left ear.

The little notch had been there since he was a puppy.

I recognized the way his front paws crossed, too.

I sent her the picture.

“Where did you get him?”

She called instead of answering in writing.

“You weren’t stable back then,” she said. “He needed somewhere permanent.”

I stood up.

“You took him from my friend’s yard?”

“I knew you’d never agree.”

“You watched me look for him.”

She said nothing.

Then she asked me not to contact her fiancé.
